sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what Docker is and why developers use it. Understand images vs containers, how Docker differs from a virtual machine, the basic workflow and its limits.

Docker packages an application together with everything it needs to run, the runtime, the libraries, the system tools, the configuration, into a single artifact that behaves the same wherever it runs.
That is the whole pitch, and it addresses a problem every team has had.

sections.title: The problem
paragraphs: An application works on a developer's laptop and fails in staging. The cause is invariably an environment difference: a different Python version, a missing system library, a config file somewhere else, a locale setting nobody thought about.
The traditional fixes were documentation nobody kept current, configuration management that drifted, or a virtual machine image that was tens of gigabytes and slow to build.
Docker's answer is to ship the environment with the application. If it runs in the container on your laptop, it runs in the same container in production, because it is the same container.

sections.title: Images and containers
paragraphs: The distinction people most often blur, and everything else depends on it.

Images are built in layers, each the result of an instruction in the Dockerfile. Layers are cached and shared. Ten images based on the same Ubuntu layer store that layer once. This is why images are far smaller in practice than their nominal sizes suggest, and why ordering Dockerfile instructions well makes rebuilds fast.

codeBlock.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27        # fetch an image
docker run -d nginx:1.27      # create and start a container from it
docker run -d nginx:1.27      # and another, from the same image

sections.title: How this differs from a virtual machine
paragraphs: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest operating system. A container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process.

Two consequences worth knowing. Containers cannot run a different kernel. Linux containers on macOS or Windows actually run inside a small Linux VM that Docker Desktop manages, which is why file sharing between host and container is slower on those platforms. And because isolation is weaker than a VM's, running genuinely untrusted code deserves a stronger boundary.

sections.title: The pieces
paragraphs: Docker Engine is the daemon that builds images and runs containers. The CLI talks to it over a socket, which is why docker commands work against a remote host just as easily as a local one.
A registry stores images. Docker Hub is the default; ECR, GCR, GitHub Container Registry and self-hosted registries all work the same way.
A volume persists data beyond a container's life. Anything written to a container's own filesystem disappears when it is removed, which surprises people exactly once.
A network lets containers reach each other. Containers on a user-defined network resolve each other by name, which is how multi-container applications are wired together.

sections.title: Containers are disposable
paragraphs: This is the mental shift that makes Docker click.

A container is not a small server you log into and maintain. It is a process you replace. Configuration comes from environment variables, data lives in volumes or a database, and logs go to stdout, so that destroying and recreating the container loses nothing.
Treating containers as long-lived pets, SSHing in, installing packages, editing files, produces exactly the environment drift Docker exists to eliminate.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Docker used for?

Packaging an application with its runtime, libraries and configuration into a single image that runs identically anywhere Docker runs. It eliminates the "works on my machine" class of problem, since the environment ships with the application rather than being recreated at each destination. In practice it is used for local development environments, CI build and test isolation, and as the deployment unit for anything running on Kubernetes, ECS or similar platforms.
What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?

An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile; a container is a running instance created from that image with its own writable layer. The relationship is like a class and an object. One image can produce any number of containers, all sharing the same underlying layers and differing only in their writable layer and running state. Images are built and pulled; containers are run, stopped and removed.
How is Docker different from a virtual machine?

A VM virtualises hardware and runs a complete guest operating system with its own kernel, typically taking gigabytes and tens of seconds to boot. A container shares the host kernel and isolates only the process, so it is measured in megabytes and starts in milliseconds. That makes containers far denser and faster, at the cost of weaker isolation, and it means a container cannot run a different kernel, which is why Linux containers on macOS or Windows run inside a small managed VM.
Do I need to learn Docker before Kubernetes?

Yes. Kubernetes orchestrates containers and assumes you already understand images, containers, ports, volumes and environment variables. A large share of Kubernetes problems turn out to be container problems in disguise: a wrong entrypoint, a missing environment variable, a process writing to a path that is not persisted. Being comfortable with docker build and docker run makes the Kubernetes learning curve considerably shorter.
Why does my data disappear when a container restarts?

Because a container's writable layer is destroyed when the container is removed, and it is not preserved across docker rm and a fresh docker run. Anything that must survive belongs in a volume, mounted into the container, or in an external service such as a database. This catches nearly everyone once, and it is the practical expression of the principle that containers are disposable. Configuration comes from environment variables and data lives outside.
Is Docker always the right choice?

No. A single simple application running fine on one server gains little from containerisation and pays the cost of another layer to understand and maintain. Desktop GUI applications are awkward in containers. Workloads needing a specific kernel or kernel modules cannot use them, since containers share the host kernel. And genuinely untrusted multi-tenant code deserves a stronger boundary than a container provides. A VM or a microVM runtime such as Firecracker.

sections.title: Why Use Docker?
paragraphs: Before we dive in totally fair question! There are a lot of tools out there. So why is Docker worth your time?
Here's the short answer: Docker makes software behave the same way, everywhere, every time. That might sound simple, but it solves one of the biggest headaches in all of software development.
Let's walk through the benefits one by one.

sections.title: Key Benefits
paragraphs: Ever sent code to a teammate and heard "it doesn't work on my machine"? That's usually because their computer is set up slightly differently than yours: different software versions, different settings, different operating system.
Docker packages your app and the environment it needs into one tidy bundle. Everyone runs the exact same thing. No more mystery bugs that only happen on certain computers.
Think of it like this: Imagine sending someone a recipe, but also sending them the exact ingredients, the exact pan, and the exact oven settings. That's Docker.
When you install lots of software on one computer, things can clash. Maybe App A needs Python 3.8 and App B needs Python 3.11, and only one can be "the default."
With Docker, each app lives in its own container, completely isolated from the others. They can't interfere with each other, even if they have conflicting requirements.
Think of it like this: Apartments in a building. Each tenant has their own space, their own rules, and they don't bother each other, even though they share the same building.
A Docker container runs on your laptop, your teammate's laptop, a cloud server, or a data center, without any changes. You build it once and it just works wherever Docker is installed.
Think of it like this: A USB drive. Plug it into any computer and your files are right there, no setup needed.

You might have heard of Virtual Machines (VMs) - they're another way to isolate software. But VMs are heavy. Each one needs its own full operating system, which eats up a lot of memory and disk space.
Docker containers are much lighter. They share the core of the host operating system, so they use far fewer resources. You could run 10 to 20 containers where a VM setup might only manage 2 to 3.
Think of it like this: VMs are like separate houses: each needs its own foundation, plumbing, and wiring. Containers are like apartments: shared infrastructure, but private spaces.
Containers start up in seconds. Virtual machines can take minutes to boot. This matters a lot when you're developing, testing, or need to quickly scale up to handle more users.
Need to handle more traffic? Just spin up more containers. Need less? Shut some down. It's that straightforward. Tools like Kubernetes can even do this automatically based on demand.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
paragraphs: Okay, benefits are great, but how does this actually show up in the real world? Here are some common scenarios:
The old way: A new developer joins your team. They spend 1 to 2 days installing the right versions of Node.js, the database, the cache server... and something always breaks.
The Docker way: They run one command docker-compose up and everything is running in minutes. Every developer on the team has the exact same setup.
Modern apps are often split into smaller, independent services one handles user logins, another handles payments, another handles product listings.
Docker is perfect for this. Each service runs in its own container, can be updated independently, and can be scaled up or down without touching the others.
Real example: An online store might have separate containers for the website, the product search, the shopping cart, and the checkout, all running together and all independently manageable.
CI/CD stands for Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment - basically, automating the process of testing and releasing your code.
Docker ensures that when your code is tested automatically, it's tested in the exact same environment it'll run in production. No more "it passed the tests but broke in production" surprises.

Got an old app that was built years ago? You don't have to rewrite it just to run it on modern servers. Wrap it in a Docker container with the old environment it needs, and it'll run just fine alongside your newer software.
Real example: An app built with Java 8 can run in a container with Java 8, even on a server that uses Java 17 for everything else.
If you build software that you sell to different businesses (SaaS), Docker lets you run a completely separate, isolated environment for each customer, same codebase, different data, total isolation.

sections.title: The Big Picture
paragraphs: Docker might feel like a lot at first, but it's really solving one core problem: making software predictable.

Once you start using it, you'll wonder how you ever managed without it. And the good news? You don't need to understand everything at once. Start small, get comfortable with the basics, and the rest will click naturally as you go.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What problem does Docker actually solve?

Environment inconsistency. An application that works on a developer's laptop and fails in staging almost always differs in something environmental: a language version, a missing system library, a config file in a different place, a locale setting. Docker ships the environment with the application, so the thing that runs in production is byte-identical to the thing that was tested. The secondary benefits, fast startup, high density, a standard deployment unit, follow from the same packaging.
Is Docker worth it for a small project?

For local development and CI, usually yes. A reproducible environment costs an afternoon to set up and removes a recurring class of problem, especially when a second person joins. For deployment it is more of a judgement call: a single application running happily on one server gains little from containerisation and pays the cost of another layer to understand. The usual tipping point is a second developer, a second environment, or a CI pipeline.
Does Docker make my application faster?

No, and it is worth being clear about that. Containers add negligible runtime overhead compared with running the process directly, but they do not speed anything up either. What gets faster is everything around the application: environment setup, deployment, scaling and rollback. On macOS and Windows, filesystem access from a container is actually slower than native, because Linux containers run inside a managed VM.
What is the difference between Docker and Kubernetes?

Docker builds and runs containers on a single machine. Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many machines. Scheduling, health checking, load balancing, rolling updates and scaling. They operate at different levels and are commonly used together: Docker to build the image, Kubernetes to run it in production. Kubernetes stopped using Docker as its runtime in version 1.24, but Docker-built images run on it unchanged because both follow the OCI standard.
Do containers replace virtual machines?

Not entirely. They solve overlapping problems with different trade-offs. Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and pack densely, but isolation is weaker and you cannot run a different kernel. VMs virtualise hardware, giving stronger isolation at the cost of size and startup time. In practice most cloud deployments run containers inside VMs, getting container density with VM-level isolation between tenants.
What are the downsides of using Docker?

Real ones worth weighing. There is a genuine learning curve covering images, layers, networking, volumes and orchestration. Persistent data needs deliberate handling, since anything written inside a container is lost when it is replaced. Debugging is less direct than on a plain host. Isolation is weaker than a VM's, so genuinely untrusted code deserves a stronger boundary. And on macOS and Windows, the hidden Linux VM makes file sharing noticeably slow for large projects.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Compare Docker containers and virtual machines on architecture, startup time, isolation and security, and learn when to choose one or use both together.
Both let you run isolated workloads on shared hardware. The difference is what gets virtualised, and everything else follows from it.
Each app needs its own complete OS copy. More apps = more wasted memory.
All apps share one OS. No duplication - containers only carry your app and its dependencies.

sections.title: The architectural difference
paragraphs: A virtual machine virtualises hardware. A hypervisor presents virtual CPUs, memory and disks, and each VM runs a complete guest operating system with its own kernel.
A container virtualises the operating system. It is a process on the host, isolated using kernel features, namespaces for what it can see, cgroups for what it can use, and it shares the host kernel.
A container has no guest OS to boot, no kernel to initialise, and no duplicated system libraries. That single fact produces every practical difference below.

sections.title: The two limits that actually matter
paragraphs: A container cannot run a different kernel. Linux containers need a Linux kernel. This is why Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows runs a hidden Linux VM: your containers are not native, and that is the reason bind-mounted file access is noticeably slow on those platforms. Windows containers exist but require a Windows host.

Isolation is weaker than a VM's. Containers share one kernel, so a kernel vulnerability is a shared attack surface, and a container escape reaches the host. A VM escape has to get through the hypervisor, which is a far smaller and more hardened boundary.

For your own code that distinction rarely matters. For genuinely untrusted multi-tenant workloads it does, which is why platforms running arbitrary customer code use VMs, or microVM runtimes like Firecracker and gVisor that combine container ergonomics with a stronger boundary.

sections.title: Are containers less secure?
paragraphs: Not inherently, but the boundary is thinner, and the defaults are more permissive than people assume.
The practical risks are usually configuration rather than architecture:
Set a non-root USER, drop capabilities, use a read-only root filesystem, and scan images. With those, containers are secure enough for the overwhelming majority of workloads.

sections.title: When to use which
paragraphs: Containers for stateless applications and microservices, CI build and test isolation, anything needing fast scaling, packaging an application with its dependencies, and local development environments.

Virtual machines when you need a different operating system or kernel, when running genuinely untrusted third-party code, for legacy applications expecting a full OS, where compliance requires hardware-level isolation, and for kernel-level work such as drivers or custom modules.

sections.title: In practice you use both
paragraphs: The framing "containers versus VMs" is mostly a false choice. Nearly every cloud deployment runs containers inside VMs:
You get container density and packaging within a VM boundary between tenants. The hypervisor isolates customers from each other; containers pack workloads efficiently inside that boundary.
That is also why "containers replaced VMs" is wrong. Containers changed how applications are packaged and scheduled; VMs remain the unit of hardware isolation underneath.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Docker Desktop on macOS runs Linux containers. How, given macOS does not have a Linux kernel?
A platform runs arbitrary code submitted by customers. Why would containers alone be a questionable isolation boundary?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the main difference between Docker and a virtual machine?

What gets virtualised. A VM virtualises hardware. A hypervisor presents virtual CPUs and disks, and each VM boots a complete guest operating system with its own kernel. A container virtualises the operating system. It is a process on the host isolated by kernel namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel. That is why containers start in milliseconds and measure in megabytes while VMs take tens of seconds and measure in gigabytes.
Are containers more secure than virtual machines?

No. VMs provide stronger isolation. All containers on a host share one kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or a container escape can reach the host and other containers, whereas a VM escape must also get past the hypervisor, a far smaller and more hardened boundary. For your own code the difference rarely matters in practice. For genuinely untrusted multi-tenant code it does, which is why such platforms use VMs or microVM runtimes like Firecracker and gVisor.
Can Docker run Windows containers on Linux, or Linux containers on Windows?

Not natively, because containers share the host kernel. Windows containers need a Windows kernel and Linux containers need a Linux one. Docker Desktop makes Linux containers work on macOS and Windows by running a lightweight Linux VM behind the scenes, on Windows it typically uses WSL 2. Everything behaves transparently, but it explains why bind-mounted file access is noticeably slower on those platforms than on native Linux.
Do containers replace virtual machines?

No, and in practice they are used together. Almost every cloud container platform runs containers inside VMs: an EKS or GKE node is a VM hosting many pods, and Fargate runs each task in its own microVM. You get container packaging and density within a VM boundary that separates tenants. Containers changed how applications are packaged and scheduled; VMs remain the unit of hardware-level isolation underneath.
When should I use a VM instead of a container?

When you need a different operating system or kernel version than the host, when running genuinely untrusted third-party code, for legacy applications that expect a full operating system with init and multiple services, when compliance requires hardware-level isolation between workloads, and for kernel-level work such as drivers or custom modules. For everything else, stateless services, CI jobs, development environments, containers are lighter and faster.
Why is Docker slow on macOS and Windows?

Because Linux containers cannot run natively there. Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM and your containers live inside it, so every bind-mounted file access crosses the boundary between the host filesystem and the VM. For a project with many small files, such as a large node_modules, this is the dominant cost. Mitigate it by bind-mounting only the source directory, keeping dependency directories in named volumes, and enabling VirtioFS in Docker Desktop's settings.

Installing Docker is usually ten minutes of clicking. The parts worth reading first are which Docker you should install, whether your employer needs to pay for it, and the three things that go wrong on nearly every machine.
Pick your platform for the step-by-step:

sections.title: Docker Desktop is not the only option
paragraphs: "Installing Docker" means different things on different systems, and the distinction matters both technically and commercially.
Docker Engine is the daemon that actually builds and runs containers. It is open source, runs natively on Linux, and is all a server needs.

Docker Desktop bundles that engine with a Linux virtual machine, a GUI, Docker Compose, a Kubernetes cluster and an update mechanism. On Windows and macOS it is effectively required, because containers are a Linux kernel feature and those systems need a Linux VM to provide one.

This catches teams out, so it is worth stating plainly. Docker Desktop requires a paid subscription for commercial use in organisations above a size threshold, at the time of writing, more than 250 employees or more than $10 million in annual revenue. Below that, and for personal use, education and open source, it remains free.
Docker Engine itself is Apache 2.0 licensed and free in all cases. The licence attaches to the Desktop product, not to containers or the engine.
If the subscription is a problem, the common alternatives are:
Most of these expose a Docker-compatible socket, so docker commands, Compose files and Testcontainers generally work unchanged.

sections.title: Requirements
paragraphs: Windows: Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, build 19041 or later. WSL 2 enabled. Hardware virtualisation enabled in BIOS or UEFI. 4 GB RAM minimum, 8 GB realistic.
macOS: macOS 12 or newer. Intel or Apple Silicon; the installer differs, so download the right one. 4 GB RAM minimum.
Linux: a 64-bit distribution with a reasonably current kernel. 2 GB RAM. You need sudo for the install and for the post-install group change.

paragraphs: On Ubuntu, docker run fails with "permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock". You run sudo usermod -aG docker $USER and try again in the same terminal. It still fails. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Is Docker Desktop free for commercial use?

Only below a size threshold. Docker Desktop requires a paid subscription for business use in organisations with more than 250 employees or more than $10 million in annual revenue; it stays free for personal use, education, non-commercial open source and smaller companies. Docker Engine, the daemon that builds and runs containers, is Apache 2.0 licensed and free in every case, which is why Linux servers and CI runners are unaffected. If the subscription is a blocker on developer machines, Podman, Colima and Rancher Desktop all expose a Docker-compatible interface.
What is the difference between Docker Desktop and Docker Engine?

Docker Engine is the daemon plus CLI that does the actual work, and on Linux it runs containers directly against the host kernel. Docker Desktop is a packaged product that bundles that engine with a Linux virtual machine, a GUI, Compose, an optional Kubernetes cluster and automatic updates. On Windows and macOS the VM is not optional, containers are a Linux kernel feature, which is why Desktop or an equivalent is required there and merely convenient on Linux.
How do I fix "permission denied" on /var/run/docker.sock?

Add your user to the docker group with sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then run newgrp docker or log out and back in. The change will not affect an already-open shell, because supplementary groups are read at login, which is why it often appears not to have worked. Understand the trade: anyone in the docker group can mount the host filesystem into a privileged container, so it is equivalent to root access on that machine. On shared systems, rootless mode is the safer arrangement.
How do I know Docker installed correctly?

Run three commands. docker --version proves the CLI is on your PATH. docker info proves the daemon is running and the CLI can reach it. docker run --rm hello-world proves the whole path works. Registry authentication, image pull, storage, container runtime and networking, and prints a confirmation message. If the first two succeed and the third fails, the problem is connectivity or registry access rather than the installation.
Why does Docker say "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon"?

The CLI is installed and nothing is listening on the socket, which is a different problem from Docker being missing. On Linux, start the service with sudo systemctl enable --now docker. On Windows or macOS, Docker Desktop is not running or is still starting. The CLI ships with the same installer and works long before the VM has finished booting, so this appears often right after installing. Check the whale icon has stopped animating before retrying.
Do I need WSL 2 to run Docker on Windows?

In practice yes. Docker Desktop's WSL 2 backend is the supported and far faster option; the older Hyper-V backend is deprecated. Run wsl --install then wsl --set-default-version 2, and make sure hardware virtualisation is enabled in the BIOS, systeminfo | findstr /C:"Virtualization" tells you whether Windows can see it. Containers then run inside a managed Linux distribution, with bind mounts noticeably faster when your project lives on the WSL filesystem rather than under /mnt/c.

sections.title: The filesystem choice that decides your build speed
paragraphs: The single most impactful setting on Windows, and it is not in any settings panel.

WSL 2 runs a real Linux filesystem. Your Windows drives are made available inside it at /mnt/c, but through a translation layer that is dramatically slower for the many-small-files access pattern that builds and node_modules produce. A project on /mnt/c/Users/you/app can build many times slower than the identical project inside the WSL filesystem.
Keep project files in the WSL 2 filesystem:
VS Code handles this properly with the WSL extension. Open the folder through Remote-WSL and the editor runs inside the distribution, so file watching and terminals are native speed.
The rule of thumb: Linux tools on Linux files, Windows tools on Windows files. Crossing the boundary is what costs you.

git clone https://github.com/acme/app.git

paragraphs: On Windows with the WSL 2 backend, docker build on a Node project takes several minutes; a colleague on Linux takes twenty seconds with the same Dockerfile. The project lives in C:\Users\you\app. What is the most likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Can I run Docker Desktop on Windows 10 or 11 Home?

Yes. The old requirement for Pro, Enterprise or Education applied to the Hyper-V backend, which needed a feature Home does not ship. The WSL 2 backend has no such dependency and is now the default and recommended option, so Home editions run Docker Desktop normally. You still need a 64-bit build 19041 or later, hardware virtualisation enabled in firmware, and WSL 2 installed.
Why is Docker so slow on Windows?

Almost always because the project lives on the Windows filesystem and is reached from WSL 2 through /mnt/c. That path crosses a translation layer that handles large sequential reads reasonably and the thousands of tiny file operations a build produces very poorly. Clone the repository inside the WSL distribution instead, cd ~ && git clone …, and open it with VS Code's Remote-WSL extension. Add a .dockerignore excluding node_modules and .git so the build context stays small either way.
How do I fix "WSL 2 installation is incomplete" or a failed WSL update?

Run wsl --install from an elevated PowerShell, then wsl --update and wsl --set-default-version 2, and reboot. If it still fails, the usual cause is virtualisation being disabled in firmware, systeminfo | findstr /C:"Virtualization" reporting No confirms it, and the setting is Intel VT-x or AMD-V, often labelled SVM Mode on AMD boards. Corporate machines sometimes also have the Virtual Machine Platform Windows feature disabled by policy, which wsl --install cannot override.
Why does Docker Desktop say the daemon is not running right after I installed it?

Because the CLI and the engine arrive together but start apart. docker.exe is on your PATH as soon as the installer finishes, while the Linux VM behind it takes a while to boot, so a command typed immediately gets "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon". Wait for the whale icon in the system tray to stop animating. If it never settles, check Docker Desktop's own diagnostics: the usual culprits are WSL 2 not fully installed or virtualisation switched off.
How much memory does Docker Desktop use on Windows, and can I limit it?

The WSL 2 VM (vmmem in Task Manager) grows as containers demand memory and by default may claim a large share of your RAM. Cap it by creating %UserProfile%\.wslconfig with a [wsl2] section setting memory=6GB and processors=4, then run wsl --shutdown and restart Docker Desktop. Note WSL 2 is slow to hand memory back to Windows even when containers stop, which is why an explicit cap is worth setting rather than relying on it releasing on its own.
What is the difference between Windows containers and Linux containers?

Linux containers are what essentially all tutorials, base images and production workloads mean by "containers", and on Windows they run inside the WSL 2 Linux VM. Windows containers are a separate mode that runs Windows processes against the Windows kernel, used for containerising .NET Framework and other Windows-only applications. You switch between modes from the Docker Desktop tray menu, and they cannot run at the same time. Unless you have specifically been asked for Windows containers, stay in Linux mode.

sections.title: Apple Silicon: the architecture problem
paragraphs: The one thing that will genuinely catch you out. An M-series Mac builds arm64 images by default. Push one to a registry, deploy it to ordinary amd64 servers, and the container dies at startup:
Nothing is wrong with the image. It is compiled for the wrong CPU.
Check what you have built:
For a one-off, build for the target instead. This uses emulation, so it is noticeably slower:
For anything shared, publish a multi-architecture image so every host pulls the variant it needs:
--push is required for multi-platform builds: the local image store cannot hold a multi-arch manifest, so --load only works for a single platform.
The same mismatch runs the other way. An amd64-only third-party image runs under emulation on your Mac and may simply refuse:
Older database images are the usual offenders. --platform linux/amd64 on docker run gets you going, at a real performance cost.

codeBlock.code: exec /app/server: exec format error

sections.title: Bind mount performance
paragraphs: The long-standing macOS complaint. Every file operation on a bind-mounted host directory crosses the VM boundary, and node_modules generates a great many of them.
Two settings in Docker Desktop are worth checking:

VirtioFS: Settings → General → Choose file sharing implementation. It is the default on current versions and substantially faster than the older gRPC-FUSE. If you have upgraded Docker Desktop over several years, you may still be on the old one.
Rosetta for x86/64 emulation: Settings → General, on Apple Silicon. Considerably faster than QEMU when you do need to run amd64 images.
Beyond that, keep dependency directories out of the mount so they live in the container's own filesystem:

codeBlock.code:
services:
  api:
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - /app/node_modules     # anonymous volume shadows the host directory

paragraphs: An image built on an M3 MacBook runs perfectly locally. Deployed to EC2, every container exits immediately with "exec /app/server: exec format error". What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my Docker image built on an M1 or M2 Mac fail on the server?

Because Docker builds for the host architecture, and Apple Silicon is arm64 while most servers are amd64. The container starts and immediately exits with exec format error, which does not mention architecture at all. Check with docker image inspect <image> --format '{{.Architecture}}'. For images others will run, build multi-architecture: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t <image> --push .. For a quick one-off, docker build --platform linux/amd64 works but runs under emulation and is slower.
Why are Docker volumes so slow on macOS?

Every file operation on a bind-mounted host directory has to cross the boundary into the Linux VM, and workloads like node_modules or a Rails app generate enormous numbers of small operations. Make sure VirtioFS is selected in Settings → General. It is the default now and much faster than the older gRPC-FUSE, but upgraded installations sometimes still use the old one. Then shadow dependency directories with an anonymous volume (- /app/node_modules in Compose) so they stay inside the VM's own filesystem.
Should I install Docker Desktop with Homebrew or the .dmg?

Either works and they install the same application. brew install --cask docker is easier to script and keeps Docker in the same update flow as your other tools, which is why it suits dotfiles and new-machine setups. The .dmg from Docker's site is more explicit about which build you are getting, which matters because Apple Silicon and Intel have separate downloads. Homebrew picks the right one for your machine automatically.
What is the free alternative to Docker Desktop on Mac?

Colima is the most common: brew install colima docker docker-compose then colima start. It runs Docker Engine inside a minimal Lima VM and exposes a standard Docker socket, so the CLI, Compose files and Testcontainers all work unchanged. Rancher Desktop and Podman Desktop are the other established open-source options, and OrbStack is a paid alternative noted for speed and low resource use. All of them exist largely because Docker Desktop requires a subscription for commercial use above roughly 250 employees or $10M revenue.
How much RAM should I give Docker Desktop on a Mac?

Start at about a quarter of your physical memory and adjust from what you actually see. On a 16 GB machine, 4 GB suits a couple of services and 8 GB is reasonable if you run a database and several containers at once. Watch real consumption with docker stats rather than guessing. Over-allocating is a genuine cost on macOS, because the VM holds that memory whether containers use it or not, and the system has less for everything else.
Why does "no matching manifest for linux/arm64" appear when pulling an image?

That image publishes no arm64 build, which is common for older or smaller third-party images, and databases in particular. Run it under emulation with docker run --platform linux/amd64 <image>, accepting that it will be slower. Check whether a newer tag is multi-arch first, docker manifest inspect <image> lists the platforms available, since most widely used images added arm64 support once Apple Silicon became common.

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A long-running container on an Ubuntu server gradually consumes all free disk space. The application writes no files. Everything goes to stdout. What is the usual cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I install docker.io or docker-ce on Ubuntu?

docker-ce, from Docker's own repository. The docker.io package in Ubuntu's archive is maintained by Debian and typically trails upstream by a significant margin, sometimes missing BuildKit features and the Compose v2 plugin entirely. Adding Docker's repository, the GPG key and sources.list.d entry in the steps above, means you get current releases and ordinary apt upgrade keeps them current. Note also that the bare docker package is an unrelated system-tray application, not what you want.
How do I run Docker without sudo on Linux?

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in, or run newgrp docker to get a shell with the new membership immediately. The step people miss is that supplementary groups are attached at login, so the shell you ran usermod in still has the old list and will keep failing. Do understand the security implication: a member of the docker group can mount the host root filesystem into a privileged container, so this is equivalent to passwordless root on that machine. On a shared server, rootless mode is the better answer.
Why does Docker keep filling up my disk?

Two causes, both fixable. Container logs are the sneaky one. The default json-file driver has no size cap, so stdout accumulates indefinitely under /var/lib/docker/containers. Set max-size and max-file in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart the daemon, remembering that the setting applies to containers created afterwards. The other is unused images, build cache and dangling volumes: docker system df shows what is reclaimable and docker system prune -a --volumes removes it.
Do I need Docker Desktop on Linux?

No. Linux runs containers natively against the host kernel, so Docker Engine alone does everything, and that is what servers and CI runners use. Docker Desktop for Linux exists and adds a GUI, a VM for consistency with colleagues on other platforms, and a bundled Kubernetes, but it also brings the commercial licence terms that Docker Engine does not have. Unless you specifically want those features, install the engine.
Why do bind mounts give permission denied on CentOS, RHEL or Fedora?

SELinux. The host directory is labelled in a way the container's process type cannot read, so files that look perfectly readable are refused. Append :z to the mount to relabel it as shared between containers, or :Z for private to this one, -v /data:/data:z. Do not disable SELinux to work around it; the relabel option exists precisely for this and takes one character. The same applies to Podman on these distributions.
How do I completely uninstall Docker from Linux?

Remove the packages, then the data directories, because purging the package deliberately leaves your images and volumes behind. On Debian and Ubuntu: sudo apt-get purge docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin, then sudo rm -rf /var/lib/docker /var/lib/containerd. On RHEL-family systems substitute dnf remove for the first command. That second step deletes every image, container and named volume on the machine, so confirm nothing there is wanted before running it.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: A plain-English guide to core Docker concepts: images, containers, Dockerfile, registry, volumes, networks, Compose, and how the client talks to the daemon.

Docker has perhaps eight ideas in it. Most early confusion comes from three of them sounding interchangeable when they are not, image, container and Dockerfile, so this page defines each precisely and shows how they connect.

sections.title: The one-line version
paragraphs: A Dockerfile is a recipe. Building it produces an image, which is a read-only template. Running an image produces a container, which is a live process. A registry is where images are stored and shared.
Everything else, volumes, networks, Compose, exists to make containers useful together.

codeBlock.code:
Dockerfile ──docker build──▶ Image ──docker run──▶ Container
                              │  ▲
                    docker push│  │docker pull
                              ▼  │
                            Registry

sections.title: Image
paragraphs: A read-only template containing everything needed to run an application: the code, the language runtime, system libraries, and the metadata describing how to start it.

An image is built from layers, one per instruction in the Dockerfile, stacked and presented as a single filesystem. Layers are what make Docker efficient: they are content-addressed and shared, so ten images built on node:22-alpine store that base exactly once on disk and pull it exactly once from a registry.

Two consequences of the layer model worth internalising early. Layers are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space in the image, and is still recoverable, which is why a deleted secret is a leaked secret. And layers are cached, so the order of instructions in a Dockerfile largely determines how fast rebuilds are.
Go deeper: Docker images and image layers.

codeBlock.code: docker images

sections.title: Container
paragraphs: A running instance of an image. If the image is the recipe, the container is the meal.

Technically it is an ordinary Linux process with restricted visibility. Namespaces give it its own view of the filesystem, process table, network stack and hostname; cgroups cap what CPU and memory it can consume. There is no virtual machine and no guest operating system. This is why a container starts in milliseconds where a VM takes a minute.

Docker adds one thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers. Every file the container creates or modifies lands there, and it is deleted with the container. That single fact explains most Docker surprises for newcomers: your database is empty again because its data lived in the writable layer of a container that no longer exists.
Containers are ephemeral by design. Treat them as disposable and keep anything that must survive in a volume.
Go deeper: Docker containers and the container lifecycle.

codeBlock.code: docker ps

sections.title: Dockerfile
paragraphs: A plain text file of instructions for building an image, executed top to bottom:

Each instruction produces a layer. The reason the package manifest is copied and installed before the source is that Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, so copying source first would reinstall every dependency on every code edit.
Go deeper: Dockerfile basics.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: Registry
paragraphs: Storage and distribution for images. GitHub, but for images rather than source. You push to share and pull to consume.

Docker Hub is the default: if you run docker pull nginx with no registry prefix, that is where it comes from. Most organisations also use a private registry. GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry. For their own images.

A tag such as 1.0 or latest is a mutable pointer to an image, not a permanent name. latest in particular is just a default tag with no special meaning; it does not track the newest version. A digest (@sha256:…) is immutable and is what you pin when reproducibility matters.
Go deeper: Docker Hub and registries.

codeBlock.code:
docker pull postgres:17
docker tag myapp:1.0 ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0
docker push ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0

sections.title: Volume
paragraphs: Storage that outlives the container. Since the container's writable layer is destroyed with it, anything that must persist, database files, uploads, goes in a volume.
Three kinds, and the distinction comes up constantly:
Go deeper: Docker volumes.

codeBlock.code:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

sections.title: Network
paragraphs: Containers on the same user-defined network reach each other by container name, which is Docker's built-in DNS at work:
The API connects to db:5432. No IP addresses, no --link, nothing to update when a container restarts with a different address.

Note that localhost inside a container means that container, not the host and not another container. Expecting localhost:5432 to reach a database in a different container is one of the most common beginner errors.
Go deeper: container networking.

codeBlock.code:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapp:1.0

sections.title: Docker Compose
paragraphs: Real applications are several containers. Compose describes them in one file so the whole stack starts together:
Compose creates a network automatically, which is why db resolves as a hostname without any extra configuration.

It is a single-host tool. Excellent for development and small deployments, not a replacement for an orchestrator. Once you need scheduling across machines, rolling updates and self-healing, that is Kubernetes.

codeBlock.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  pgdata:

sections.title: Client and daemon
paragraphs: One more piece, because it explains a whole class of error messages.
The docker command is a client. It does almost nothing itself. It sends requests over a socket to the daemon (dockerd), which builds images, runs containers and manages storage.

So Cannot connect to the Docker daemon means the CLI is installed and working, and nothing is listening. Start the service. And permission denied ... docker.sock means the daemon is running but your user cannot talk to its socket.
It also explains why the build context is sent to the daemon: the daemon may not be on your machine at all.

codeBlock.code: docker CLI ──/var/run/docker.sock──▶ dockerd ──▶ containerd ──▶ runc ──▶ your process

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Postgres container is started with docker run, data is written, then the container is removed and recreated from the same image. The data is gone. Which concept explains this?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?

An image is a read-only template: the application, its runtime, its libraries and the metadata describing how to start it, stored as a stack of layers. A container is a running instance created from that image, with a thin writable layer on top for anything it changes. One image can back any number of containers simultaneously, each with its own writable layer, in the same way one class can have many instances. The practical consequence is that images persist and containers are disposable.
Where does data written inside a container go?

Into the container's writable layer, which exists only as long as the container does. Remove the container and every file it created is removed with it, which is why a database restarted from the same image comes back empty. Mount a named volume at the path that matters (-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data) and the data lives outside the container lifecycle. Bind mounts do the same thing with a specific host directory, which is what you usually want in development.
What is a Docker layer and why does it matter?

Each Dockerfile instruction produces one layer, a filesystem diff, and the image is those layers stacked into a single view. They matter for three reasons. They are shared, so images built on the same base store and transfer it once. They are cached, so ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing makes rebuilds dramatically faster. And they are immutable, so a file added in one layer and deleted in a later one still occupies space and remains extractable from the image.
What is a Docker registry and is Docker Hub the only one?

A registry stores and distributes images, the way a Git host stores repositories. Docker Hub is the default, docker pull nginx with no prefix goes there, and hosts official images for most common software. It is not the only option, and most organisations push their own images to a private registry such as GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry or Azure Container Registry. Prefixing the image name with a hostname selects one: ghcr.io/acme/myapp:1.0.
Do I need Docker Compose or Kubernetes?

Compose if you are running several containers on one machine. A local development stack, a small single-server deployment. It defines services, networks and volumes in one file and starts them together, and it is the right tool most of the time. Kubernetes when you need containers scheduled across multiple machines with rolling updates, self-healing and autoscaling. They solve different problems, and starting with Compose costs nothing if you later move: the concepts transfer directly.
Why can't my container reach another container on localhost?

Because localhost inside a container refers to that container and nothing else. Each one has its own network namespace and its own loopback interface. Put both on the same user-defined network and use the container name as the hostname: docker network create appnet, start each with --network appnet, then connect to db:5432. Compose does this for you automatically, which is why service names work as hostnames there without any configuration.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what a Docker image is, how layers and tags work, how to shrink images, and how to reclaim disk space by removing dangling images and old tags.
An image is a read-only template containing a filesystem and the metadata needed to run it. Containers are created from images; images are built from Dockerfiles or pulled from registries.
Nearly everything worth knowing about images comes down to layers.

sections.title: Layers
paragraphs: Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. A set of filesystem changes stacked on the one before. The final image is those layers combined and presented as one filesystem.
docker history is the first command to reach for on any size problem. It shows exactly which instruction added the weight, which is rarely the one people expect.
Three properties follow, and between them they explain most image behaviour.
Ten images built on the same base store that base once. This is why docker images can list ten images at 200 MB each while docker system df reports far less total disk:
A rebuild reuses every layer up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. Instruction order therefore determines build speed:
Reversing those two blocks means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile performance mistake and costs minutes on each build.
A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is still in the image. The later layer adds a whiteout marker hiding it; the bytes remain in the earlier layer and still ship.
This catches nearly everyone once, usually with apt-get caches:

codeBlock.code: docker history nginx:1.27

sections.title: Tags and digests
paragraphs: A tag is a mutable pointer. nginx:1.27 today and nginx:1.27 next month can be different images, because the maintainer can repoint it.
For reproducible builds, and anything security-sensitive, pin the digest.

At minimum, never deploy latest. It is not special, just the default tag name, and it means your deployment depends on whatever was most recently pushed. Two deploys of "latest" can run different code, and a rollback has nothing specific to return to.
Tagging adds a name to an existing image rather than copying it:
Both names now point at one image ID.

codeBlock.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # mutable
docker pull nginx@sha256:a1b2c3...     # immutable content hash

sections.title: Reducing image size
paragraphs: Size affects pull time, registry storage, and cold start on every platform that schedules containers. Three techniques, in order of impact.

Choose a smaller base. node:22 is roughly 1.1 GB; node:22-alpine around 150 MB; distroless smaller still. Alpine uses musl rather than glibc, which occasionally breaks native modules. Test rather than assume.
Use a multi-stage build, so build tooling never reaches the final image:
The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a scratch image is a few megabytes.
Add a .dockerignore. Without one, COPY . . sends node_modules, .git and every local artifact into the build context and often into the image:
This speeds builds too, since the context is uploaded to the daemon before the build starts.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: Dangling images and reclaiming disk
paragraphs: That <none> entry is a dangling image. The previous build of myapp, orphaned when the tag moved to the newer image. It still occupies disk.
Rebuilding the same tag repeatedly produces one every time, which is why disk usage climbs steadily during development and why Docker eventually reports no space left on device.

One thing prune does not touch: container logs. A long-running container using the default json-file driver with no rotation can write tens of gigabytes to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log. If docker system prune frees less than expected, that is usually where the space went:
Put that in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart Docker to cap it.

codeBlock.code: docker images

sections.title: Registries
paragraphs: Docker Hub is the default, so nginx means docker.io/library/nginx. Any other registry must be named explicitly.

Two practical notes. Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls, which a busy CI pipeline hits quickly. Authenticate, or mirror base images into your own registry. And a push only transfers layers the registry does not already hold, so pushing a rebuilt image is usually fast.

codeBlock.code:
docker login registry.example.com
docker push registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2
docker pull registry.example.com/myapp:1.4.2

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile downloads a 500 MB archive in one RUN and deletes it in the next. The image is still 500 MB larger than expected. Why?
A server reports "no space left on device". docker system prune -a removes several images but frees little space. What is the likely cause?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?

An image is a read-only template made of stacked filesystem layers; a container is a running instance created from it with its own thin writable layer. One image can produce any number of containers, all sharing the same underlying layers, which is why running ten containers from one image consumes very little extra disk. Images are built and pulled; containers are run, stopped and removed.
How do I reduce my Docker image size?

Three things, in order of impact. Switch to a smaller base, node:22-alpine is around 150 MB against roughly 1.1 GB for node:22. Use a multi-stage build so compilers and development dependencies stay in the build stage and never ship. Add a .dockerignore so node_modules, .git and local artifacts are not copied in. Then run docker history to see which instruction is actually adding the weight, because it is often not the one you would guess.
Why doesn't deleting files reduce my Docker image size?

Because layers are additive and all of them ship together. A file created in one layer and removed in a later one is hidden by a whiteout marker, but its bytes remain in the earlier layer and are still part of the image. Anything downloaded and then deleted must be handled within a single RUN instruction chained with &&, so only the net result is committed. The same applies to package manager caches. Clean them in the same RUN that installed the packages.
What are dangling images and is it safe to delete them?

They are the <none> entries in docker images. Previous builds whose tag was reassigned to a newer image, leaving them unreferenced. They are entirely safe to remove, and docker image prune does exactly that. They accumulate quickly during development because every rebuild of the same tag creates one, which is the usual reason disk usage climbs steadily and eventually produces "no space left on device".
Why did docker system prune not free much disk space?

Almost certainly container logs, which prune never touches. With the default json-file log driver and no rotation, a long-running container can write tens of gigabytes to /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log. Check that directory's size directly. Fix it by setting "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restarting Docker. Named volumes are the other common culprit, since they are only removed with --volumes.
Should I use the latest tag?

No. latest is not special. It is simply the default tag name, pointing at whatever the maintainer most recently pushed, which can change without warning. Deploying it means two deploys of the same nominal version can run different code, and a rollback has no specific artifact to return to. Pin an explicit version tag, and for anything security-sensitive pin the digest with image@sha256:..., which is a content hash and genuinely immutable.

sections.title: Docker Image Name
paragraphs: A Docker image name is basically an address. It tells Docker three things: where the image lives, what it is, and which version you want.
The full format looks like this:
When you run docker pull nginx, Docker automatically expands it to docker.io/library/nginx:latest. The short name is just a convenient.
Here's a simple analogy: imagine ordering a book. The registry is the bookstore, the repository is the book title, and the tag is the book's edition.

codeBlock.code: registry/repository:tag

sections.title: Breaking Down a Real Docker Image Name
paragraphs: Let's look at some real examples to make this concrete:

codeBlock.code:
# Just the image name - Docker fills in the rest automatically
nginx

# Same image, but with a specific version
nginx:1.25

# Lightweight version of the same image
nginx:1.25-alpine

# Full name written out completely
docker.io/library/nginx:latest

# An image published by a user or organization on Docker Hub
username/myapp:v2.0.0

# An image stored on a private company registry
myregistry.company.com/backend/api:production

# An image hosted on Google's registry
gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0

# An image on GitHub's registry, identified by a commit hash
ghcr.io/owner/repo:sha-abc1234

sections.title: What Is a Docker Tag?
paragraphs: A tag is a label that points to a specific version of an image. The catch? Tags are mutable which means not permanent. They're more like sticky notes: someone can move them to point to a different image at any time. This is why using the latest tag in production is risky:
Bottom line: For anything serious (production apps, CI/CD pipelines, team projects), always pin to a specific version tag. It saves you from mysterious bugs caused by unexpected version changes.

codeBlock.code:
# Today this might download Node.js version 18
# Tomorrow it might download Node.js version 22
docker pull node:latest

# This will ALWAYS download exactly Node.js 20.11.0
docker pull node:20.11.0

sections.title: How to Tag Docker Images Like a Pro
paragraphs: Good tagging habits make your images easier to manage, understand, and reproduce. There are really only four questions a good tag can answer: what version is this, how big/lean is it, where does it go, and what exact code is inside it. Each strategy below answers one of those questions. Once you know which question you're answering, the right tag style becomes obvious.

Semantic versioning follows the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format, and it's the closest thing Docker has to a universal standard. Think of the three numbers as a report card, read left to right from "biggest change" to "smallest change":

Easy way to remember it: the more numbers in the tag, the more "locked in" you are. One number is loose and will silently change under you; three numbers never move. For production, always reach for the full three-number tag. You want to know exactly what you're running, not "whatever the latest patch happens to be today."
Many official images ship in different "flavors" of the same software, built on different base operating systems. The variant name usually shows up after a dash:

Easy way to remember it: picture ordering coffee. bookworm is the large cup with everything included: more room to work, more disk space used. slim is a medium cup with just the essentials trimmed out. alpine is the tiny espresso shot: fast and small, but it's brewed differently (Alpine uses musl instead of glibc), so it doesn't always taste right with every recipe. That's why Alpine images are popular for production (small, fast to pull, smaller attack surface) but are also the most likely to cause a strange compatibility bug, so always test before committing to one.

This kind of tag isn't really describing the code itself; it's a destination label, like a shipping sticker on a box. On its own it doesn't tell you what's inside, only where it's headed, which is why the best environment tags combine the destination with a real version, like staging-v2.1.0 above: now the tag answers both "where" and "what."
Easy way to remember it: if you can answer the question "where is this going?" just by reading the tag, it's an environment tag.

A Git commit SHA is a unique fingerprint for one exact snapshot of your source code. Baking it into the tag means that if something breaks in production six months from now, you can read the tag straight off the running container, paste that SHA into git show, and see the exact lines of code that were live at that moment. No guessing, no "which version was this again?"

Easy way to remember it: SHA tags are your evidence trail. They don't replace a version number (you can have both, like v1.4.2-sha-a3f8c2d) - they just guarantee you can always trace a running container back to one specific commit.

In practice, most real-world tags combine two or three of these in one string - myapp:staging-v2.1.0 and myapp:v1.4.2-sha-a3f8c2d are both already doing that above. Pick the question you most need answered when someone looks at the tag six months from now, and build from there.

codeBlock.code:
myapp:1.0.0   # A specific patch release (most precise)
myapp:1.0     # Floats to the latest 1.0.x release
myapp:1       # Floats to the latest 1.x.x release

sections.title: The Most Permanent Way to Reference an Image: Digests
paragraphs: Every image has a unique fingerprint called a digest, a long hash that looks like this:
Unlike tags (which can change), a digest never changes. It will always refer to the exact same image content, forever.
Use digests when you need 100% reproducibility. For example, in regulated industries, security-sensitive environments, or when debugging a production incident months after the fact.

codeBlock.code: docker pull nginx@sha256:7144f7bab3d4c2648d7e59409f15ec52a18006a128c733fcff20d3a4a54ba44a

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: Tag an Image Yourself
paragraphs: The best way to understand tagging is to try it. Here's a quick exercise:
Notice that tagging doesn't create a new copy of the image; it just creates new pointers to the same data. Docker is efficient like that.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Download the official nginx image
docker pull nginx

# Step 2: Give it a new tag called webserver:v1.0
docker tag nginx webserver:v1.0

# Step 3: Give it another tag called webserver:stable
docker tag nginx webserver:stable

# Step 4: Confirm all three tags exist (they all point to the same image)
docker images | grep -E "nginx|webserver"

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What happens if I don't specify a tag?
Docker automatically uses latest. This is fine for quick experiments but risky in production because latest can point to a different image version over time.
Can I create my own tags for someone else's image?
Yes! The docker tag command lets you add your own tags to any image you've pulled. The tags only exist locally on your machine unless you push them to a registry.
What's the difference between a registry and a repository?

A registry is the entire hosting platform (like Docker Hub). A repository is one specific image within that platform (like the nginx repo on Docker Hub). A registry can hold thousands of repositories.
Are Alpine images always better?

Not always. Alpine images are smaller and faster to pull, but they use a different C library (musl instead of glibc), which can cause compatibility issues with some software. Test Alpine images thoroughly before using them in production.

sections.title: What Is Docker Hub?
paragraphs: Docker Hub is the internet's largest public library of container images. Think of it like the App Store but instead of apps, it stores pre-built Docker images that you can download and run instantly.

It's also Docker's default registry, which means Docker looks there automatically whenever you pull an image without specifying where it should come from. Docker Hub hosts millions of images, ranging from bare-bones operating systems to fully configured databases, web servers, and developer tools.

sections.title: What Kind of Images Can You Find There?
paragraphs: Not all Docker Hub images are the same quality. There are three tiers you should know about:

Official Images are the gold standard. They're maintained by Docker itself or directly by the software's creators. They have no username prefix in their name (just nginx, not someuser/nginx), they're updated regularly with security patches, and they come with proper documentation.
Here are some of the most commonly used official images organized by category:
Verified Publisher Images are published by well-known companies, like Bitnami, Elastic, or HashiCorp. They have a company namespace (e.g. bitnami/postgresql) but are still trustworthy.

Community Images are published by regular developers and organizations. Quality varies enormously. Before using one, check how many stars it has, how many times it's been pulled, and when it was last updated.
The safe approach: start with official images whenever possible, then verified publishers, and treat community images with a healthy dose of skepticism.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do I need an account to use Docker Hub?
No, you can pull public images without logging in. But creating a free account increases your rate limit from 100 to 200 pulls every 6 hours, and lets you push your own images.
How do I know which tag to use?
Check the Tags tab on Docker Hub for the image you want. For production, always use a specific version tag (like redis:7.2) rather than latest, since latest can change at any time.
Are community images safe to use?
Some are, some aren't. Red flags include: no recent updates, very few stars/pulls, and no documentation. Always prefer official or verified publisher images when they exist.

sections.title: How to Pull Images
paragraphs: Pulling an image just means downloading it to your local machine. Here are the most common ways to do it:

One thing that makes Docker smart: it downloads images in layers, and it caches those layers locally. If two images share the same base OS layer, Docker only downloads it once. This saves both time and disk space as you accumulate more images.

codeBlock.code:
# Download the latest version of nginx (simplest form)
docker pull nginx

# Download a specific version (always safer in production)
docker pull postgres:16

# Download a lightweight Alpine variant
docker pull python:3.12-alpine

# Download from a different registry (not Docker Hub)
docker pull gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0

# Download by digest (the most permanent, unchangeable reference)
docker pull ubuntu@sha256:77906da...

sections.title: What Does the Pull Output Actually Mean?
paragraphs: When you pull an image, you'll see something like this:

Each line represents a layer - a piece of the image stacked on top of the previous one. If you've already pulled another image that shares a layer, you'll see Already exists instead of Pull complete. That's Docker being efficient and reusing what's already on your machine.

codeBlock.code:
7.2: Pulling from library/redis
a480a496ba95: Pull complete      ← downloading the base OS layer
e2677dab5ef2: Pull complete      ← installing packages on top
ca5b0a5ac559: Pull complete      ← adding the Redis binary itself
Digest: sha256:e96c03a6dda7...
Status: Downloaded newer image for redis:7.2

sections.title: How to Search for Images
paragraphs: You can search Docker Hub right from your terminal without opening a browser:
The output looks something like this:
The [OK] in the OFFICIAL column is your signal that this is an officially maintained image. Images without it are community-contributed.
For seeing all available version tags, reading documentation, or checking security scan results, head to hub.docker.com and search there. The web UI gives you a lot more detail than the CLI.

codeBlock.code:
# Search for any image by name
docker search nginx

# Limit results to the top 5
docker search --limit 5 postgres

# Only show images with at least 50 stars
docker search --filter stars=50 redis

# Only show official images
docker search --filter is-official=true python

sections.title: Practice: Search and Pull from Docker Hub
paragraphs: The best way to get comfortable with these commands is to try them yourself. Here's a quick walkthrough:
Notice the [OK] badge in the search results. This confirms Redis is an officially maintained image. And after pulling, docker images should show redis with the 7.2 tag, its image ID, and size.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: Search for official Redis images on Docker Hub
docker search --filter is-official=true redis

# Step 2: Pull a specific version - never just "latest" in real projects
docker pull redis:7.2

# Step 3: Confirm the image downloaded successfully
docker images | grep redis

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Do I need to run docker pull before docker run?

No - docker run automatically pulls the image if it isn't already on your machine. docker pull is useful when you want to download an image ahead of time, or update a locally cached image to its newest version.
How do I see all the images I've already pulled?
Run docker images (or docker image ls). It lists every image stored locally along with its tag, ID, size, and when it was created.
Why does my pull say Already exists for some layers?
That's Docker reusing a cached layer from a previously pulled image. It's completely normal and actually a good thing: it means Docker is being efficient and not re-downloading data you already have.
What's the difference between a tag and a digest?

A tag (like redis:7.2) is a human-readable label that can be reassigned over time. A digest (like ubuntu@sha256:779...) is a cryptographic fingerprint that is permanently tied to one exact version of an image. Use digests when you need a guarantee that nothing will ever change.
Why do some image names have a slash and others don't?

Images without a slash (like nginx) are official images maintained by Docker or the software vendor. Images with a slash (like bitnami/postgresql) belong to a user or organization. The slash separates the namespace from the image name.
I'm on a Mac with Apple Silicon and the image isn't working. Why?
Some images are only built for linux/amd64 (Intel architecture). Pull with --platform linux/amd64 to explicitly request that version, and Docker Desktop will run it through emulation automatically.

sections.title: List & Inspect Images
paragraphs: You've pulled a few images. Maybe you've built one too. Now the natural question is "what's actually sitting on my machine, and how do I understand what's inside these images?"
Docker gives you a handful of commands to answer exactly that. This guide walks through all of them in plain English.

sections.title: How to See All Your Local Images
paragraphs: The most basic command is docker images. Run it and you'll get a table of every image stored on your machine:
Here's what each column actually means:

One thing worth knowing about the SIZE column: if two images share layers (for example, both use the same Ubuntu base), that shared layer is only stored once on disk, but it still gets counted in each image's size. So the total disk usage is usually less than the sum of all the sizes you see listed.

codeBlock.code:
# List all images
docker images

# Identical alternative
docker image ls

# Include intermediate build layers
docker images -a

# Show only image IDs
docker images -q

# Filter by repository name
docker images nginx

# Filter by reference (name + tag)
docker images "nginx:1.25"

sections.title: Filtering and Formatting the Image List
paragraphs: As you pull more images, the list gets long. These commands help you to filter the images:
Dangling images are the most common thing to clean up. They're leftover layers from previous builds that no longer have a name or tag attached to them.

codeBlock.code:
# Show dangling images (untagged leftovers from old builds)
docker images --filter dangling=true

# Show images created before a specific image
docker images --filter before=nginx:latest

# Show images created after a specific image
docker images --filter since=alpine:3.18

# Custom output (show only name, tag, and size)
docker images --format "{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} - {{.Size}}"

sections.title: How to Inspect What's Inside an Image
paragraphs: docker images tells you what you have. docker inspect tells you everything about a specific image. It returns a detailed JSON document packed with metadata:
The --format flag uses Go templates to pull out just the field you care about, so you don't have to wade through the entire JSON output. Here's a taste of what the full output contains:

The most practically useful fields for beginners are ExposedPorts (which port your container will listen on), Env (what environment variables are pre-configured), and Cmd (what command runs when you start the container).

codeBlock.code:
# See the full details of an image
docker inspect nginx:latest

# Extract just the default command the image runs
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Cmd}}' nginx

# See all environment variables baked into the image
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Env}}' nginx

# See which ports the image expects to be open
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.ExposedPorts}}' nginx

# List all the layers that make up the image
docker inspect --format='{{.RootFS.Layers}}' nginx

sections.title: Hands-On Practice: List and Inspect an Image
paragraphs: After step 2, you should see map[80/tcp:{}] which tells you nginx listens on port 80. That's the port you'll need to map when you run the container.

codeBlock.code:
# Step 1: See all images currently on your machine
docker images

# Step 2: Inspect the nginx image to find which port it exposes
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.ExposedPorts}}' nginx

# Step 3: Check the default command nginx runs on startup
docker inspect --format='{{.Config.Cmd}}' nginx

sections.title: How to See an Image's Layer History
paragraphs: Every Docker image is built up from layers, one on top of the other, like a stack of transparent sheets. docker history shows you every layer, what command created it, and how much space it takes:
A few things to notice here:
Layers showing 0B are metadata-only, things like setting an environment variable (ENV) or declaring a port (EXPOSE). They don't add any actual files to the image, so they take up no space.
The big layers (58.4MB, 80.4MB) are where real files were added, like installing nginx, or laying down the base OS filesystem.
<missing> in the IMAGE ID column is completely normal. It just means the intermediate layer isn't stored as a standalone image on your machine, only the final result is kept.

codeBlock.code: docker history nginx:latest

sections.title: How to Check How Much Disk Space Docker Is Using
paragraphs: Docker can quietly eat up a lot of disk space over time because of old images, stopped containers, unused volumes, and build cache all accumulate. This command gives you a clear overview:

The RECLAIMABLE column is the key one. It shows how much space you could free up by cleaning things out. In this example, 890MB of build cache can be fully reclaimed since none of it is actively in use.

codeBlock.code:
# Quick summary
docker system df

# Full breakdown with details
docker system df -v

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What's the difference between docker images and docker image ls?
They do exactly the same thing. docker image ls is the newer, more structured syntax that Docker introduced as part of a broader command reorganization.
Why does CREATED show a date from weeks ago even though I just pulled the image?
The CREATED date is when the image was built by whoever published it, not when you downloaded it. If you pulled nginx today but the image was built two weeks ago, you'll see two weeks ago.
What are dangling images and should I delete them?

Dangling images are untagged layers left behind from previous builds. For example, when you rebuild an image and the old version loses its tag. They're generally safe to delete with docker image prune.
Why do I see <missing> in docker history output?
It means the intermediate layer isn't stored as a separate image on your machine, only the final image is kept locally. This is normal and doesn't indicate anything is broken.
The sizes in docker images add up to way more than my actual disk usage. Why?

Because shared layers are counted in each image's size but only stored once on disk. Two images that both use the same Alpine base will each show the Alpine layer in their size, but your disk only holds one copy of it. docker system df gives a more accurate picture of real disk usage.
