sections.title: Why Container Storage Is Temporary
paragraphs: Each container has its own isolated filesystem layer. It's writable while the container runs, but it's tied to that container's lifecycle. Remove the container, lose the data. For anything that needs to outlive a container like database data, user uploads, logs; you need to store it outside the container using one of Docker's three storage options:

sections.title: Named Volumes
paragraphs: Named volumes are stored in Docker's own managed area on your host (/var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux). You don't need to know the exact path, Docker manages it for you.
The -v syntax is volume-name:path-inside-container. Docker creates the volume if it doesn't exist yet.
The key benefit is that data survives container removal:
The container is gone but the volume isn't. Named volumes only get deleted when you explicitly remove them.

codeBlock.code:
# Create a volume explicitly
docker volume create mydata

# Or let Docker create it automatically on first use
docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16

sections.title: Bind Mounts
paragraphs: A bind mount maps a specific folder or file from your host machine directly into the container. Changes on either side are reflected instantly which means no rebuild, no restart. Edit a file in your editor, and the container sees it immediately. This is the standard way to run a development server in Docker without rebuilding the image on every change.

codeBlock.code:
# Mount your current project directory into the container
docker run -d \
  --name my-app \
  -v $(pwd):/app \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  node:20-alpine \
  sh -c "cd /app && npm run dev"

# Mount a directory to capture logs on the host
docker run -d \
  -v $(pwd)/logs:/app/logs \
  my-app

sections.title: Named Volume vs Bind Mount
paragraphs: The short version: named volumes for data that needs to last, bind mounts for files you're actively working with.

sections.title: tmpfs Mounts
paragraphs: It is a In-Memory Storage and can be used for sensitive data (tokens, secrets, session data) that should never be written to disk. A tmpfs mount exists only in memory. It's fast, it's never written to disk, and it disappears completely when the container stops. It is perfect for temporary files or sensitive in-memory data.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  --tmpfs /app/tmp:rw,size=64m \
  my-app

# List all volumes
docker volume ls

# Inspect a volume (find its actual location on the host)
docker volume inspect pgdata

# Remove a specific volume
docker volume rm mydata

# Remove all volumes not attached to any container
docker volume prune

# Remove without being prompted to confirm
docker volume prune -f

sections.title: Sharing a Volume Between Containers
paragraphs: Multiple containers can mount the same volume at the same time:
One writer, multiple readers is safe. Multiple containers writing to the same files simultaneously can corrupt data, so design it carefully.

codeBlock.code:
# Create a shared volume
docker volume create shared-logs

# App container writes logs to it
docker run -d --name app -v shared-logs:/app/logs myapp

# Log shipper reads from it (read-only)
docker run -d --name logshipper -v shared-logs:/logs:ro fluentd

sections.title: Backing Up and Restoring Volumes
paragraphs: Since named volumes are managed by Docker, backing them up means spinning up a temporary container to read and archive the data:
This pattern is using a lightweight Alpine container to read or write volume contents and is the standard Docker approach for volume backups.

codeBlock.code:
# Back up a volume to a tar file on your host
docker run --rm \
  -v pgdata:/source:ro \
  -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /source .

# Restore from that backup into a volume
docker run --rm \
  -v pgdata:/target \
  -v $(pwd):/backup \
  alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata-backup.tar.gz -C /target

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: If I delete a container, does its volume get deleted too?

No. Named volumes persist independently of containers. The volume and its data stick around until you explicitly remove it with docker volume rm or docker volume prune. This is a common source of confusion for beginners, and also why docker volume prune is a useful cleanup command.
What's the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?

A named volume is managed by Docker and you can use it by name and Docker handles where it lives on your host. A bind mount is a specific path on your host machine that you map into the container. Named volumes are more portable and better for persistent data; bind mounts are more convenient for development because you can see and edit the files directly.
Why is my bind mount showing an empty directory inside the container?

If the container image already has files at the mounted path, the bind mount will hide them. Either pre-populate your host directory with the needed files, or use a named volume which merges with the image's existing content at that path.
Can two containers write to the same volume at the same time?

They can, but it's risky. Concurrent writes to the same files from multiple containers can corrupt data as there's no built-in locking. The safe pattern is one writer and multiple read-only readers (using :ro).
How do I find where a named volume is stored on my host?

Run docker volume inspect <name> and look at the Mountpoint field. On Linux it's usually under /var/lib/docker/volumes/. On Mac and Windows, volumes live inside the Docker Desktop VM, so you can't browse them directly from Finder/Explorer, that's why named volumes are better than bind mounts for those platforms.
What happens to my data if I run docker volume prune?

It permanently deletes all volumes that aren't currently attached to at least one container (running or stopped). Before running it, check docker volume ls and make sure you're not about to lose anything important. There's no undo.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Pass docker environment variables with the -e flag and --env-file, check them in a running container, and learn why secrets need a safer approach.

sections.title: Docker Environment Variables & Container Configuration
paragraphs: Your database URL, API keys, port numbers, feature flags, none of these should be hardcoded into your image. The moment you do that, you need a different image for development, staging, and production. Instead, pass configuration in at runtime using environment variables. Same image, different config, any environment.

sections.title: Passing Environment Variables with -e
paragraphs: The -e flag sets a single environment variable when starting a container:
You can also forward a variable directly from your host shell, just omit the =value part. This is useful in CI/CD pipelines where secrets are already available as environment variables on the runner.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -e NODE_ENV=production my-app

# Multiple variables, one -e flag per variable
docker run \
  -e NODE_ENV=production \
  -e PORT=3000 \
  -e LOG_LEVEL=warn \
  my-app

sections.title: Using an Env File with --env-file
paragraphs: When you have more than a few variables, managing them with individual -e flags gets messy. Use a .env file instead:

Never commit .env files with real secrets to version control. Add .env to your .gitignore immediately. Use a .env.example file with placeholder values to document what's needed without exposing real credentials.

codeBlock.code:
# .env
NODE_ENV=production
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db:5432/myapp
REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379
LOG_LEVEL=info
JWT_SECRET=my-super-secret-key

sections.title: Viewing Environment Variables in a Running Container
paragraphs: This is useful for verifying your variables were passed correctly, and a good reminder that env vars are visible to anyone who can run docker inspect.

codeBlock.code:
# Print all env vars from inside the container
docker exec my-app env

# Or check from the host without exec-ing in
docker inspect my-app --format='{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}'

sections.title: Setting Defaults in Your Dockerfile
paragraphs: Use ENV in your Dockerfile to define sensible defaults that can be overridden at runtime:
When someone runs your image without specifying these variables, the defaults apply. When they do specify them, their values win:
These two Dockerfile instructions are easy to mix up:

codeBlock.code:
ENV PORT=3000
ENV LOG_LEVEL=info

sections.title: How to Handle Secrets Safely
paragraphs: Environment variables are convenient, but they're not the most secure option for sensitive values because they show up in docker inspect output and in process listings. For production, consider better alternatives:
If environment variables are your only option (common in development), at minimum: never log them, never bake them into the image, and use --env-file so they don't appear in your shell history.
In production Docker Swarm environments, Docker Secrets keep sensitive values out of environment variables entirely:
The secret is mounted as a file at /run/secrets/db_password inside the container, not an environment variable, so it won't appear in docker inspect.

codeBlock.code:
# Create a secret
echo "my-db-password" | docker secret create db_password -

# Use it in a service
docker service create \
  --name my-app \
  --secret db_password \
  my-app:latest

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What's the difference between ARG and ENV in a Dockerfile?

ARG is only available during the image build process, and it can't be read by your running application. ENV sets a variable that persists into the running container and can be overridden at runtime with -e. Use ARG for build customization (version numbers, build flags) and ENV for runtime configuration defaults.
Is it safe to put secrets in environment variables?

For local development, it's acceptable. For production, it's not ideal because environment variables show up in docker inspect, process listings, and crash dumps. Use Docker Secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or a secrets manager for anything sensitive in production.
Can I see what environment variables a container is running with?
Yes, run docker inspect <container> and look for the Env section, or run docker exec <container> env to print them from inside. This means anyone with Docker access on that host can see those values.
What happens if the same variable is set in both --env-file and -e?
The -e flag wins. It takes precedence over values in the env file, so you can use --env-file as a base and selectively override specific variables with -e.
Should I commit my .env file to Git?

Never commit a .env file that contains real credentials. Instead, commit a .env.example file with all the variable names but placeholder values, this documents what's needed without exposing anything sensitive.
How do I pass environment variables in Docker Compose?
In your docker-compose.yml, use the environment key for inline values or env_file to load from a file. It's the same concepts as -e and --env-file in docker run.

sections.title: Docker Cleanup & Pruning
paragraphs: Every container you run, every image you pull, every build you run, it all piles up quietly in the background. Left unchecked, it's not unusual to find Docker eating 20 to 30GB of disk space after a few weeks of active development. Therefore, it becomes important to clean it up safely.

sections.title: See What's Taking Up Space First
paragraphs: Before deleting anything, check what you actually have:
docker system df output:
The RECLAIMABLE column is your target, it shows exactly how much space you can get back without affecting anything currently in use.

codeBlock.code:
# Show running containers
docker ps

# Show ALL containers, including stopped ones
docker ps -a

# Count how many stopped containers are sitting around
docker ps -aq -f status=exited | wc -l

# Disk usage breakdown across all Docker objects
docker system df

sections.title: Removing Containers
paragraphs: You can't remove a running container without -f. Either stop it first with docker stop, or force-remove it with docker rm -f.

The most effective way to avoid container buildup is to never let them accumulate in the first place. Add --rm to any container you don't need to keep. Use --rm for one-off commands, CI tasks, data migrations, quick tests or anything you won't need to revisit. It's the single best cleanup habit you can build.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove a stopped container
docker rm my-container

# Remove multiple at once
docker rm web db cache

# Force remove a running container (in background, it stops first, then deletes)
docker rm -f my-container

# Remove a container and its anonymous volumes
docker rm -v my-container

sections.title: Removing Images
paragraphs: Old and unused images are usually the biggest disk consumers:
Dangling images are the untagged <none> images you see in docker images, they're leftover intermediate layers from previous builds. Safe to delete.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove a specific image
docker rmi nginx:1.24

# Remove multiple images
docker rmi nginx:1.24 node:18

# Force remove (even if a stopped container references it)
docker rmi -f old-image:v1

# Remove dangling images (untagged layers left over from builds)
docker image prune

# Remove ALL images not used by any container
docker image prune -a

# Skip confirmation
docker image prune -a -f

sections.title: Removing Volumes
paragraphs: docker volume prune permanently deletes data. Always run docker volume ls first to make sure you're not about to wipe something important. There's no undo.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove a specific volume
docker volume rm mydata

# Remove all volumes not attached to any container
docker volume prune

# Skip confirmation
docker volume prune -f

sections.title: Removing Networks
paragraphs: Unused networks are safe to prune as they hold no data, just configuration.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove a specific network
docker network rm my-network

# Remove all unused networks
docker network prune

sections.title: Build Cache Cleanup
paragraphs: Build cache is almost always the biggest and safest thing to delete:
Build cache is 100% safe to delete. The only consequence is that your next build starts from scratch and takes longer, but subsequent builds will cache again normally.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove all build cache
docker builder prune

# Remove cache older than 48 hours
docker builder prune --filter "until=48h"

# Skip confirmation
docker builder prune -f

sections.title: The Nuclear Option: docker system prune
paragraphs: When you want to clean everything at once:
Don't run docker system prune -a --volumes unless you're sure. It removes every container, image, and volume not currently in use, including volumes with data you might still need.

codeBlock.code:
# Remove stopped containers, dangling images, unused networks, build cache
docker system prune

# Also remove unused volumes
docker system prune --volumes

# Also remove ALL unused images (not just dangling ones)
docker system prune -a

# Full cleanup, no prompts
docker system prune -a --volumes -f

sections.title: A Practical Cleanup Routine
paragraphs: Daily during active development:

codeBlock.code:
docker container prune -f    # Stopped containers gone
docker builder prune -f      # Build cache cleared

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I check how much disk space Docker is using?
Run docker system df. It gives a breakdown by object type (images, containers, volumes, build cache) with a RECLAIMABLE column showing how much you can safely free up.
What's the difference between docker rm and docker container prune?

docker rm removes specific containers you name. docker container prune removes all stopped containers in one go. Use docker rm when you want to be selective; use prune when you want to bulk-clean everything that's no longer running.
Will docker image prune delete images I still need?

docker image prune (without -a) only removes dangling images, untagged layers leftover from builds. It won't touch images that have a tag. Adding -a removes all images not currently used by any container (running or stopped), so if you have images you want to keep but aren't using right now, skip the -a flag.
Is it safe to delete build cache?

Yes, always. Build cache just speeds up future builds. Deleting it means your next build takes longer (a cold build), but it won't break anything. Subsequent builds will recreate the cache layer by layer.
What does --rm do and when should I use it?

--rm tells Docker to automatically delete the container as soon as it exits. Use it for anything you run once and don't need to revisit like one-off commands, scripts, tests, migrations. It's the best way to prevent stopped containers from piling up.
I ran docker volume prune and lost my database data. How do I recover it?

Unfortunately, docker volume prune permanently deletes volume data and there's no built-in recovery. This is why checking docker volume ls before pruning is so important. Going forward, set up regular volume backups.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how to write a Dockerfile: FROM, COPY, RUN and CMD, layer caching, .dockerignore, multi-stage builds, HEALTHCHECK and the mistakes that bloat images.

A Dockerfile is a script of instructions for building an image. Each instruction produces a layer, and understanding that one fact explains most of what makes a Dockerfile fast or slow, large or small.

sections.title: A complete example
paragraphs: That trailing . is the build context. The directory sent to the Docker daemon before the build starts. It is not the Dockerfile location, which is why a large context slows builds even when nothing is copied.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies first. This layer is cached until package files change
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Source last. Changes here do not invalidate the install above
COPY . .

ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000

USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: The instructions
paragraphs: Pin a specific version. FROM node means node:latest, which changes without warning and makes your build non-reproducible.
Use COPY. It does exactly one thing: copy files from the context.

ADD additionally fetches URLs and auto-extracts local tar archives. Both behaviours are surprising. The auto-extraction in particular has caused real bugs when a .tar.gz was meant to be copied verbatim. Use COPY, and RUN curl when you genuinely need to download something.
Each RUN is a layer, and layers are additive. A file created in one and deleted in a later one still ships in the image:
--no-install-recommends alone often removes tens of megabytes.
ARG values are passed with --build-arg and are not secret. They appear in docker history. Never pass a token or password as a build arg. Use BuildKit secrets instead:
This is documentation. It records which port the application listens on for humans and tooling; it does not open or publish anything. Publishing happens at run time with -p 3000:3000.

Containers run as root by default, which is unnecessary for almost every application and a real risk if the container is compromised. Most official images provide a non-root user. Place USER after any instruction needing root, such as package installation.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
FROM node:22-alpine AS build        # named stage, for multi-stage
FROM node@sha256:abc123...          # pinned by digest, fully reproducible

sections.title: Layer caching is the whole game
paragraphs: Docker reuses cached layers up to the first instruction whose inputs changed, then rebuilds everything after it. Order instructions from least to most frequently changing:
Putting COPY . . before RUN npm ci means every source edit reinstalls every dependency. It is the most common Dockerfile mistake and costs minutes on each build.

For RUN instructions, the cache key is the command string, not what it produces. RUN apt-get update stays cached indefinitely even as upstream packages change, which is why it must be chained with the install in the same instruction.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine          # changes rarely
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./        # changes when dependencies change
RUN npm ci --omit=dev        # expensive. Keep it cached
COPY . .                     # changes on every commit
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: .dockerignore
paragraphs: Without one, COPY . . pulls in node_modules, .git, local .env files and build output:
This reduces image size, speeds up the build by shrinking the context, and, importantly, stops local secrets being baked into the image.

codeBlock.code:
node_modules
.git
.env
dist
*.log
Dockerfile
.dockerignore

sections.title: Multi-stage builds
paragraphs: Build in one stage, ship from another. Tooling never reaches the final image:

The compiler, dev dependencies and source are all absent from what ships. For compiled languages the effect is dramatic. A Go binary in a scratch image is a few megabytes against a 900 MB build image.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: HEALTHCHECK
paragraphs: docker ps then shows healthy or unhealthy. --start-period is the one that matters, without enough of it, a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

codeBlock.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile has COPY . . before RUN npm ci. Changing one line of source reinstalls every dependency. Why?
A Dockerfile has EXPOSE 3000 and the app listens on 3000, but curl to localhost:3000 on the host fails after docker run. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?

COPY copies files and directories from the build context into the image, and does nothing else. ADD does the same but additionally fetches remote URLs and automatically extracts local tar archives. Both extras are surprising in practice. A .tar.gz you meant to copy verbatim gets unpacked instead. Use COPY for local files and RUN curl when you genuinely need to download something, which also lets you verify a checksum in the same layer.
Why is my Docker build slow every time?

Almost certainly instruction order. Docker caches layers up to the first instruction whose inputs changed and rebuilds everything after it, so COPY . . placed before your dependency install means every source edit reinstalls all dependencies. Copy the package manifest and lockfile first, run the install, then copy the source. A missing .dockerignore compounds it by sending node_modules and .git into the build context on every build.
What does EXPOSE actually do?

Only documentation. It records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling such as docker run -P, which publishes all exposed ports to random host ports. It does not open a port, publish one, or affect networking in any way. Reaching the application from the host requires -p 3000:3000 at run time, and the container is reachable by other containers on the same network whether or not EXPOSE is present.
What is the difference between ENV and ARG?

ARG defines a build-time variable available only while the image is being built, and it is gone at runtime. ENV sets an environment variable baked into the image and present in every container started from it. A critical caveat: ARG values appear in docker history, so they must never carry secrets. Use BuildKit secret mounts, which make a value available during a single RUN without recording it in any layer.
Should I use a multi-stage build?

Almost always, for anything with a build step. Compilers, development dependencies and source code stay in the build stage and never reach the shipped image, which usually cuts size dramatically. A Go binary in a scratch image is a few megabytes against a 900 MB build environment. It also reduces attack surface, since a compiler in a production image is a tool an attacker can use. The cost is a few extra lines.
Why does my container run as root and how do I change it?

Because that is the default when no USER instruction is given, and most base images do not set one. It is unnecessary for nearly every application and increases the damage a compromise can do, particularly combined with a mounted host path. Add USER node, or whichever non-root user your base image provides, after any instructions that need root, such as package installation. On Kubernetes you can additionally enforce it with runAsNonRoot: true, which turns a root image into a visible startup failure rather than a silent risk.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Choose the right Dockerfile FROM base image: alpine vs slim vs full, pinning tags and digests, multi-stage FROM, platform targeting and the scratch image.

Every Dockerfile begins with FROM. It decides the operating system, the C library, the package manager, the size of the image, and how much of your security patching is someone else's job. It is the most consequential line in the file.

codeBlock.code:
FROM <image>
FROM <image>:<tag>
FROM <image>@<digest>
FROM <image>:<tag> AS <stage-name>

sections.title: Choose the variant, not just the image
paragraphs: Most official images publish several variants, and the difference is dramatic:
Those numbers are the uncompressed local size; what you push is smaller. The ranking is what matters, not the digits.
Alpine uses musl libc rather than glibc, and that one substitution causes most Alpine surprises.

Node.js packages with native bindings, bcrypt, sharp, canvas, ship prebuilt binaries for glibc. On Alpine they compile from source, which needs build tooling in the image and adds minutes to the build.

Python is the sharp one. The manylinux wheels on PyPI are glibc-only, so pip install on Alpine builds nearly everything from source. A pandas install that takes 20 seconds on python:3.12-slim can take many minutes on python:3.12-alpine, and the resulting image is frequently larger because the compiler had to come along. For Python, default to -slim, not -alpine.
There have also been long-standing reports of musl's DNS resolver behaving differently from glibc's under certain cluster configurations. Rare, but memorable when it happens.
Alpine remains an excellent choice for Go, Rust, and anything without native extensions.
Distroless images are glibc-based, so no musl surprises, but contain no shell, no package manager and no coreutils. That removes most of the toolkit an attacker would reach for after breaking in.

The trade is debugging: docker exec -it <container> sh does not work, because there is no sh. Use the :debug tag variant when you need a shell, or attach an ephemeral debug container in Kubernetes with kubectl debug.
scratch is an empty filesystem. Only a statically linked binary can run in it, which is why CGO_ENABLED=0 is essential, without it the Go binary links against libc and dies immediately:

That message names no file because the missing file is the dynamic linker. Two other things scratch lacks that catch people out: TLS root certificates and timezone data. Copy them in when you need them:

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12
COPY --from=build /app /app
WORKDIR /app
CMD ["server.js"]

sections.title: Pin the tag. Then pin the digest.
paragraphs: A tag is a mutable pointer. node:22 today and node:22 next month are different images, which is how a build that worked yesterday fails this morning with no commit in between.
A digest is content-addressed and cannot change. That is what you want for production and for anything a compliance process looks at.

The obvious objection, "then I never get security patches", is answered by automation, not by leaving the tag loose. Renovate and Dependabot both raise pull requests that bump a pinned digest, which gives you the update and a reviewable record of it.
For everything else, rebuild against the tag periodically:
Without --pull, a locally cached base image can be months old and your "fresh" build inherits every one of its CVEs.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:latest              # changes without warning
FROM node:22                  # still a moving target: 22.x advances
FROM node:22.11.0-alpine3.20  # a specific release
FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:bf77dc26e48ea95fca9d1aceb5acfa69d2e546b765ec2abfb502975f1a2d4def

sections.title: Multi-stage: each FROM starts a stage
paragraphs: Only the final stage ships. Compilers, dev dependencies and source stay behind.
Name stages with AS. You can reference them by index, but COPY --from=build survives someone inserting a stage above it and COPY --from=0 does not.
Build a single stage when you want to debug it:
--from also reads from images you never based anything on, which is often the cleanest way to obtain one binary:

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: Platform targeting
paragraphs: Use this sparingly. It pins every stage to one architecture. The better pattern lets BuildKit tell each stage what it is building for:

Building on an Apple Silicon Mac and deploying to amd64 servers without this produces an exec format error at container start, which is an architecture mismatch rather than anything wrong with the image.
You want to pull both node:20 and node:20-alpine, then compare their sizes side by side. Which sequence of commands is correct?

codeBlock.code: FROM --platform=linux/amd64 node:22-alpine

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A team switches a Python service from python:3.12-slim to python:3.12-alpine expecting a smaller image. The build takes eight minutes instead of forty seconds, and the final image is larger. What happened?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Should I use Alpine or slim for my Docker base image?

It depends entirely on the language. Alpine uses musl instead of glibc, which is fine for Go and Rust but costly for anything relying on prebuilt native binaries. For Python specifically, prefer -slim: PyPI's manylinux wheels are glibc-only, so Alpine forces pip to compile from source, which makes builds many times slower and often produces a larger image than the slim variant. Node.js sits in between. Alpine is fine until you need bcrypt or sharp, at which point -slim saves the trouble.
Why shouldn't I use the latest tag in a Dockerfile?

Because a tag is a mutable pointer, not a fixed image. node:latest resolves to something different over time, so the same Dockerfile and the same source produce different images on different days, and a build can break with no change on your side. The same applies more subtly to node:22, which advances through 22.x. Pin a full version tag at minimum, and a digest when reproducibility genuinely matters. Then use Renovate or Dependabot to bump it, so updates arrive as reviewable pull requests.
What is a distroless image and when should I use one?

A distroless image contains your application's runtime and nothing else, no shell, no package manager, no coreutils. It is glibc-based, so it avoids Alpine's musl compatibility problems while still being small, and the missing tooling removes most of what an attacker would use after gaining execution. The cost is debugging: docker exec … sh fails because there is no shell. Use the :debug tag variant when you need one, or kubectl debug to attach an ephemeral container in Kubernetes.
Why does my FROM scratch container exit immediately with "no such file or directory"?

The binary is dynamically linked and the file the kernel cannot find is the dynamic linker, not your program, which is why the message names nothing useful. Build statically: for Go that means CGO_ENABLED=0 go build, for Rust the musl target. Two other things scratch does not provide are TLS root certificates and timezone data, so copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt from the build stage if your application makes HTTPS calls, or use gcr.io/distroless/static, which includes both.
How do I pin a Docker base image to a digest?

Run docker inspect node:22-alpine --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' to get the digest, then write FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:… in the Dockerfile. A digest is content-addressed, so it always resolves to the exact same bytes. Keep the human-readable tag alongside it for legibility. Pair this with Renovate or Dependabot, which raise a pull request when the underlying tag moves, that way you get reproducible builds and still receive security patches, rather than trading one for the other.
What is the difference between multiple FROM lines and multiple Dockerfiles?

Multiple FROM lines create stages within a single build, and only the final stage becomes the image. Earlier stages exist purely so later ones can copy artefacts out with COPY --from=build, which is how compilers and dev dependencies stay out of what ships. That is almost always better than maintaining separate build and runtime Dockerfiles, because the stages share one file, one build command and one cache. Use --target when you want to stop at an intermediate stage for debugging or testing.

commonPitfalls: Deploying changes to production without dry-running or checking execution plans.
Neglecting automated healthchecks, probe timeouts, and resource quota boundaries.
Failing to pin immutable versions or image digests in production manifests.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn when to use COPY vs ADD in a Dockerfile. Covers build context, --chown and --chmod, COPY --from, the dependency-manifest pattern and .dockerignore.

COPY and ADD both bring files from the build context into the image. The short answer is use COPY, but the long answer is worth knowing, because ADD has picked up genuinely useful features recently and the old advice to never touch it is now slightly out of date.

sections.title: The build context decides what is copyable
paragraphs: Before either instruction runs, Docker packages a directory and sends it to the daemon. That directory is the build context, the . at the end of docker build -t myapp ., and it is the only thing COPY can read from.
That transferring context line is worth watching. If it reports hundreds of megabytes, you are shipping node_modules and .git to the daemon on every single build before any instruction executes.
This is also why the most confusing COPY error exists:

Nothing outside the context is reachable, no matter how valid the path looks on your machine. The fix is to build from a directory that contains everything you need and point at the Dockerfile explicitly:

codeBlock.code: docker build -t myapp .

sections.title: COPY: the default choice
paragraphs: Source paths are relative to the build context. Destination paths are absolute, or relative to WORKDIR.
If /app does not already exist, this creates a file named /app containing your server code. The next instruction that expects /app to be a directory then fails with something that looks unrelated:
Two safe habits: always write a trailing slash on directory destinations, or set WORKDIR /app first and copy to ..
COPY copies the contents of a source directory, not the directory itself:
Getting this backwards produces a /app/src/src nesting that is easy to miss until something 404s at runtime.

codeBlock.code:
# Single file
COPY server.js /app/server.js

# Into a directory. The trailing slash matters
COPY server.js /app/

# Multiple sources always need a directory destination
COPY package.json package-lock.json /app/

# Wildcard
COPY *.json /app/

# Entire directory
COPY ./src /app/src

sections.title: COPY --chown
paragraphs: Copied files are owned by root by default. If your container runs as a non-root user, and it should, that user may not be able to write to its own application directory:
--chown sets ownership as part of the same layer, which costs nothing. A separate RUN chown -R duplicates every file into a new layer and can double your image size:
Numeric IDs are more portable, since a named user has to exist in the image already:
Referencing a user that does not exist yet fails the build:
Create the user with RUN adduser before the COPY that references it.

codeBlock.code: Error: EACCES: permission denied, open '/app/logs/app.log'

sections.title: COPY --chmod
paragraphs: This saves a RUN chmod layer and, more usefully, works regardless of the permissions the file had on the machine that built it, which is what makes a Windows checkout produce a working entrypoint script.
--chmod needs BuildKit, the default builder in current Docker. On an older engine, add the syntax directive at the very top of the Dockerfile:

codeBlock.code:
COPY --chmod=755 entrypoint.sh /entrypoint.sh
COPY --chmod=644 config.yaml /app/config.yaml

sections.title: COPY --from
paragraphs: --from reads from another build stage, or from an entirely separate image, instead of the build context:
Pulling a single binary out of a published image is the other common use, and it beats a curl and checksum dance:

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: The dependency-manifest pattern
paragraphs: The highest-value COPY pattern in any Dockerfile. Copy the manifest, install, then copy source:
Reverse those and every one-character source edit reinstalls every dependency, because the COPY . . layer is invalidated and everything after it rebuilds. The same shape applies in every ecosystem:

You are writing a Dockerfile based on node:20-alpine with WORKDIR /app. You want to copy package.json into the image owned by the "node" user, install dependencies, and then copy the rest of the source, also owned by "node". Which snippet is correct?

codeBlock.code:
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .

sections.title: ADD: what it actually does
paragraphs: ADD is COPY plus three behaviours.
Auto-extracts local tar archives. This is the one legitimate reason to reach for it:
It is also the behaviour that bites people. A .tar.gz you meant to ship verbatim gets unpacked instead, and nothing warns you. Note the asymmetry. A local archive is extracted, a remote one is not.
Fetches URLs, now with checksum verification. The long-standing objection to ADD <url> was that you could not verify what you downloaded. Modern Dockerfile syntax fixes that:
Clones a Git repository:
ADD <url> still cannot clean up after itself. The downloaded file is in that layer permanently. When you need to download, use, and discard something, one RUN does all three in a single layer:
The rule: COPY by default. ADD for local tar extraction, or for a URL when the file is genuinely meant to stay in the image and you pin a --checksum.

codeBlock.code: ADD rootfs.tar.gz /

sections.title: .dockerignore
paragraphs: COPY . . takes everything in the context unless you exclude it. The syntax mirrors .gitignore:
Three things it buys you: local secrets never get baked into a layer, the context shrinks so builds start faster, and irrelevant file changes stop invalidating your cache.
Negation works, which is how you ship one file out of an excluded directory:
The classic .dockerignore failure is over-excluding. A blanket * or an overly broad pattern silently hides a file COPY needs, and the error names the file rather than the ignore rule:
If a COPY cannot find a file that plainly exists, check .dockerignore before anything else.

codeBlock.code:
# Dependencies. Reinstalled inside the image anyway
node_modules/
vendor/
__pycache__/
.venv/

# Version control
.git/
.gitignore

# Secrets and local config
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.key

# Build artifacts
dist/
build/
target/

# IDE and OS noise
.vscode/
.idea/
.DS_Store

# Tests and docs
tests/
coverage/
*.md

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile at services/api/Dockerfile has COPY ../../shared/config.json /app/. The file definitely exists on disk, but the build fails with "not found". Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between COPY and ADD in a Dockerfile?

COPY copies files and directories from the build context into the image and does nothing else. ADD does the same, and additionally extracts local tar archives automatically, downloads remote URLs, and clones Git repositories. The extras are why the default advice is COPY. An archive you meant to ship intact gets silently unpacked. Use ADD deliberately, for local tar extraction or a URL download you pin with --checksum, and COPY for everything else.
Why does my COPY fail with "forbidden path outside the build context"?

Because the source path climbs above the directory you passed to docker build. Docker packages that directory and sends it to the daemon before any instruction runs, so anything outside it simply does not exist as far as COPY is concerned. Regardless of how valid the path looks in your shell. Build from a directory that contains everything you need and point at the Dockerfile with -f, for example docker build -f services/api/Dockerfile -t api . from the repository root.
How do I fix "permission denied" after adding USER to my Dockerfile?

The copied files are still owned by root, and your non-root user cannot write to them. Add --chown to the COPY instructions, COPY --chown=node:node . ., which sets ownership as part of that layer at no cost. Avoid fixing it with a separate RUN chown -R, because that rewrites every file into a brand new layer and can roughly double the image size. If the user does not exist in the base image, create it with RUN adduser before the COPY that references it.
Why is COPY saying a file is not found when it clearly exists?

Check .dockerignore first. An over-broad exclusion pattern removes the file from the build context, and the resulting error names the file rather than the rule that hid it, typically failed to compute cache key: "/package.json": not found. The other cause is the source path pointing outside the build context. Both mean the same thing: the daemon never received that file.
Do I need a .dockerignore file?

Effectively yes, before your first COPY . .. Without one the entire directory is sent to the daemon on every build, so node_modules and .git slow the build before an instruction runs, local .env files and private keys get baked into layers where anyone with the image can read them, and unrelated file changes invalidate your layer cache. At minimum exclude node_modules/, .git/, .env* and your build output directory.
What does COPY --from do?

It reads from somewhere other than the build context. Either an earlier stage in the same Dockerfile (COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist) or a completely separate image (COPY --from=hashicorp/terraform:1.9 /bin/terraform /usr/local/bin/). The first is what makes multi-stage builds work, letting compilers and dev dependencies stay behind in the build stage. The second is often a cleaner way to obtain a binary than downloading and verifying it yourself, since the image is already versioned and pinnable.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how the Dockerfile RUN instruction works, including shell vs exec form, apt-get best practices, same-layer cleanup, cache mounts, secrets and heredocs.

RUN executes a command during the build and commits the result as a layer. It installs packages, compiles code, creates users and sets permissions. How you write it is most of the difference between a 50 MB image and a 500 MB one.
The single fact that explains nearly every RUN mistake: layers are additive and immutable. Anything a RUN creates is permanent, and a later RUN that deletes it only hides it.

sections.title: Shell form and exec form
paragraphs: Shell form is the normal choice for RUN, because &&, pipes, redirects and variable expansion all need a shell. Exec form matters when the base image has no shell at all.
Variable expansion is the trap:
(This is the opposite of the advice for CMD and ENTRYPOINT, where exec form is what you want so the process receives signals.)

codeBlock.code:
# Shell form. Runs via /bin/sh -c "..."
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl

# Exec form. Runs the binary directly, no shell
RUN ["apt-get", "install", "-y", "curl"]

sections.title: Installing packages
paragraphs: Three non-negotiables here:
If an install hangs waiting for input, you have hit a package with an interactive prompt:
Prefer setting it inline on the one RUN that needs it, as a persistent ENV it also affects anyone who later docker execs into the container.
--no-cache skips storing the index entirely, so there is no cleanup step.

codeBlock.code:
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      curl \
      git \
      ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: Why cleanup must be in the same layer
paragraphs: A layer is a filesystem diff. Deleting a file in a later layer records a whiteout entry. The file disappears from the container's view while still occupying space in the layer below, and still being readable by anyone who pulls the image and inspects it layer by layer.
That last part matters for more than size. A secret written and then deleted in a later RUN is still extractable from the image.
The fat instruction names itself. Here build-essential is 178 MB that almost certainly belongs in a build stage rather than the shipped image.

codeBlock.code:
# Wrong. The apt lists are permanently in layer 1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Right. Created and removed inside one layer
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

sections.title: Cache mounts make rebuilds fast
paragraphs: The upgrade most Dockerfiles are missing. A BuildKit cache mount keeps a package or compiler cache on the builder between builds, without putting a single byte in the image:
Note that with a cache mount you deliberately stop deleting the lists. The mount is not part of the image, so there is nothing to clean up.
The same pattern pays off everywhere dependency resolution is slow:
A cold install that took 90 seconds typically drops to a few. The caveat is that the cache lives on whichever builder ran the build, so CI needs a persistent or exported cache to see the benefit.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt/lists,sharing=locked \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl

sections.title: Secrets belong in a mount, not a layer
paragraphs: The value exists for the duration of that one instruction and is written to no layer. Passing the same token as an ARG records it in docker history for anyone who pulls the image.

codeBlock.code:
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmtoken \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npmtoken) npm ci

sections.title: Pipes hide failures
paragraphs: Shell form runs under /bin/sh -c, and in a pipeline only the last command's exit status counts. This build succeeds even when the download 404s:
curl fails, sh receives empty input and exits 0, the layer commits, and the missing tool surfaces at runtime instead. Fix it for the whole file:
On Alpine, where bash may be absent, do it per instruction:

codeBlock.code: RUN curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | sh

sections.title: Heredocs for multi-command blocks
paragraphs: Much easier to read than a wall of && \, and set -eux gives you fail-fast behaviour plus an echo of each command in the build log. Requires BuildKit, which is the default in current Docker.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN <<EOF
set -eux
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
EOF

sections.title: Creating users and directories
paragraphs: Prefer COPY --chown over a trailing RUN chown -R wherever you can, chown on copied files rewrites every one of them into a new layer.

You want a single RUN instruction in a Dockerfile based on ubuntu:24.04 that updates apt, installs curl and wget without recommended packages, and cleans up the package lists afterward, all in one layer. Which instruction is correct?

codeBlock.code:
# Debian
RUN groupadd -r appgroup \
 && useradd -r -g appgroup -d /app -s /sbin/nologin appuser

# Alpine
RUN addgroup -S appgroup \
 && adduser -S -G appgroup appuser

RUN mkdir -p /app/logs && chown -R appuser:appgroup /app

sections.title: Cache-friendly ordering
paragraphs: RUN layers are cached on the instruction string, not on what the command produces. Order from least to most frequently changing:
When you genuinely need to bust the cache:

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

# System packages. Change rarely
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Changes only when requirements.txt does
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r requirements.txt

# Changes on every commit
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile downloads a 400 MB SDK in one RUN and deletes it in the next RUN. The final image is still around 400 MB larger than expected. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?

RUN executes during docker build and commits the result as an image layer, so its effects are baked in permanently. This is where you install packages and compile code. CMD sets the default command executed when a container starts from the finished image, and it produces no layer content. A Dockerfile normally has several RUN instructions and exactly one CMD. If you find yourself wanting to "run something when the container starts", that is CMD or ENTRYPOINT, not RUN.
Why doesn't deleting files in a later RUN reduce my image size?

Because each instruction commits an immutable filesystem diff. A delete in a later layer writes a whiteout marker, which makes the file invisible inside the container while the actual bytes stay in the layer that created them and still travel with the image. Put the creation and the deletion in one RUN joined with &&, or move the whole step into a build stage that never ships. The same mechanism is why a secret written and later deleted is still recoverable from the published image.
Why should apt-get update and apt-get install be in the same RUN?

Docker caches a RUN layer on its command string, not on what the command actually produced. As a separate instruction, RUN apt-get update keeps its cached layer indefinitely, so a later install runs against a package index that may be months old. Producing Version '…' for '…' was not found or silently installing outdated packages. Chaining them means any change to the install list re-runs the update too.
How do I make Docker builds faster without making the image bigger?

Use BuildKit cache mounts. RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci keeps the package cache on the builder between builds while writing nothing into the image, and the same works for pip, Go module and build caches, and apt. Combine that with ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing, and copying dependency manifests before source code. In CI you will also need a persistent or exported cache, since the mount lives on whichever builder ran the build.
Why does my build succeed even though a command inside RUN failed?

Shell form runs under /bin/sh -c, and in a pipeline only the final command's exit status is reported. So RUN curl -fsSL https://… | sh succeeds even when curl 404s, because sh reads empty input and exits cleanly. Add SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"] near the top of the Dockerfile, or prefix the individual instruction with set -o pipefail &&. Using set -eux inside a heredoc block gives the same protection plus a readable build log.
How do I find which instruction made my image so large?

docker history <image> --no-trunc lists every layer with its size and the instruction that created it, largest offenders usually being obvious at a glance. docker image inspect and tools like dive go further if you need to see individual files. Once you have identified it, the fix is normally one of three things: clean up inside the same RUN, add --no-install-recommends, or move the whole step into a build stage and copy only the artefact forward with COPY --from.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile, how to combine them, when to use exec vs shell form, and how to override both at runtime.
Both define what runs when a container starts, and the difference between them is one of the most frequently asked Docker questions.
ENTRYPOINT defines what runs. CMD defines the default arguments.
Everything else follows from how each behaves when you pass arguments to docker run.

sections.title: The behavioural difference
paragraphs: That is the whole distinction. A worked example:

codeBlock.code:
FROM alpine
CMD ["echo", "hello"]

sections.title: Using them together
paragraphs: This is the idiomatic pattern, and it is what most well-built images do:
ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD supplies a default argument the user can override. The container always runs Python, but which script is up to the caller.
Another common shape. A tool with a sensible default subcommand:

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
CMD ["app.py"]

sections.title: Exec form vs shell form
paragraphs: Both instructions accept two syntaxes, and choosing wrongly causes a real and confusing bug.
Use exec form. The signal behaviour is the reason, and it is not a small detail.
With shell form, /bin/sh is PID 1 and your application is a child process. docker stop sends SIGTERM to PID 1, the shell, which does not forward it. Your application never learns it should shut down.
Docker waits 10 seconds, then SIGKILLs everything.

The symptoms are recognisable: containers always take exactly 10 seconds to stop, in-flight requests are cut off, and graceful shutdown code never runs. On Kubernetes the same problem makes every rolling deploy drop connections.
Variable expansion and shell operators only work in shell form:
The fix that gives you both is exec, which replaces the shell rather than spawning a child:
exec means the shell process is replaced by node, so node becomes PID 1 and receives signals normally.

codeBlock.code:
CMD ["node", "server.js"]      # exec form. JSON array
CMD node server.js             # shell form

sections.title: Entrypoint scripts
paragraphs: The standard pattern for images needing setup before the main process:

Two details make this work. exec "$@" runs whatever CMD supplied, replacing the script so the application ends up as PID 1 with working signal handling. And because CMD is still overridable, docker run myimage sh drops you into a shell while still running the setup first.
Omitting exec, writing just "$@", is the single most common bug in entrypoint scripts. The script stays PID 1, signals go to it, and graceful shutdown breaks.

codeBlock.code:
#!/bin/sh
set -e

# Setup: wait for dependencies, run migrations, render config
until nc -z "$DB_HOST" 5432; do
  echo "waiting for database"
  sleep 1
done

# Hand over. Exec replaces this script, so the app becomes PID 1
exec "$@"

sections.title: Overriding at runtime
paragraphs: --entrypoint is how you get a shell in an image whose entrypoint immediately runs something else. Invaluable for debugging a container that exits instantly.
Note the asymmetry: --entrypoint takes only the executable. Arguments to it go after the image name.

codeBlock.code:
docker run myimage other-arg              # overrides CMD
docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh myimage   # overrides ENTRYPOINT

sections.title: Inheritance
paragraphs: A child image's ENTRYPOINT resets the inherited CMD to null. If you set ENTRYPOINT in a derived image and rely on the base image's CMD, you get nothing:

codeBlock.code:
FROM someimage        # has ENTRYPOINT ["app"] and CMD ["--serve"]
ENTRYPOINT ["wrapper"]
# CMD is now empty. You must restate it
CMD ["--serve"]

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile uses CMD node server.js in shell form. Every docker stop takes exactly 10 seconds and the application's shutdown handler never runs. Why?
An image has ENTRYPOINT ["python"] and CMD ["app.py"]. What runs for docker run myimage other.py?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in Docker?

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD defines the default arguments passed to it. The practical difference shows at runtime: arguments given to docker run replace CMD entirely but are appended to ENTRYPOINT. So an image with ENTRYPOINT ["python"] and CMD ["app.py"] runs python app.py by default and python other.py when you pass other.py. The executable is fixed and the caller controls the arguments.
Should I use CMD or ENTRYPOINT?

Use both together for an image that is one specific tool: ENTRYPOINT fixes the binary, CMD provides overridable defaults. Use CMD alone for a general-purpose image where users may want to run arbitrary commands, such as a language runtime image. Use an ENTRYPOINT script ending in exec "$@" when setup must happen before the main process. Waiting for a dependency, rendering configuration, running migrations.
What is the difference between exec form and shell form?

Exec form is the JSON array syntax, CMD ["node", "server.js"], and runs the binary directly as PID 1. Shell form, CMD node server.js, runs it via /bin/sh -c, making the shell PID 1 with your application as a child. Exec form is strongly preferred because only PID 1 receives signals, with shell form your application never sees SIGTERM and graceful shutdown silently never happens. Shell form does allow variable expansion and pipes, which exec form does not.
Why does my container take 10 seconds to stop?

Because your application is not receiving SIGTERM, so docker stop waits the full grace period and then SIGKILLs it. The usual cause is shell form: /bin/sh is PID 1 and does not forward signals to its child. Switch to exec form so your process is PID 1. If you have an entrypoint script, make sure it ends with exec "$@" rather than plain "$@", since without exec the script remains PID 1 and absorbs the signal.
How do I use an environment variable in CMD?

Exec form does not expand variables, CMD ["node", "app.js", "--port", "$PORT"] passes the literal string $PORT. The safe way to get expansion without losing signal handling is CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec node app.js --port $PORT"]. The exec is essential: it replaces the shell process with your application so it becomes PID 1. Plain shell form expands the variable but leaves the shell as PID 1 and breaks shutdown.
How do I override ENTRYPOINT to debug a container?

docker run --entrypoint /bin/sh -it myimage replaces the entrypoint and drops you into a shell, which is the standard way to inspect an image whose entrypoint exits immediately or crashes. Note that --entrypoint accepts only the executable. Any arguments go after the image name. For a distroless image with no shell at all, copy the filesystem out with docker create and docker cp instead.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn the difference between ENV and ARG in a Dockerfile, how ARG scoping works, why neither is safe for secrets, and how ARG affects the build cache.

Both define variables, but they live in different phases of the image's life. ARG exists only while the image is being built. ENV is baked into the image and present in every container started from it.
Getting them backwards produces one of two outcomes: a variable your application cannot see at runtime, or a secret permanently readable by anyone who pulls the image.

sections.title: The core difference
paragraphs: That fourth row is the one people miss. ARG is gone at runtime, which feels private, but the value it was given is written into the image's build metadata regardless.

sections.title: ENV: runtime configuration
paragraphs: One instruction for several variables, because each ENV is its own layer. The older space-separated form (ENV NODE_ENV production) still parses but is deprecated and cannot set multiple values. Use =.
Values are visible to every RUN that follows, to the container's main process, and to any later docker exec session:
ENV sets a default, and -e overrides it without a rebuild:

That is the point of it: the image ships sensible defaults, the deployment overrides what differs. Precedence runs docker run -e → Compose environment: → Compose env_file: → Dockerfile ENV, with the leftmost winning.
ENV also expands earlier variables, which is how you extend PATH:
Good uses: default ports and log levels, PATH-style variables, tool configuration such as PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 or PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1.
Never: API tokens, passwords, connection strings with credentials. Those come from the orchestrator at runtime.

codeBlock.code:
ENV NODE_ENV=production \
    PORT=3000 \
    LOG_LEVEL=info

sections.title: ARG: build-time parameters
paragraphs: With no default and no --build-arg, the value is simply empty. The build does not fail. That silent emptiness is worth guarding when the value matters:

codeBlock.code:
ARG APP_VERSION=1.0.0
ARG GIT_COMMIT

RUN echo "Building $APP_VERSION from $GIT_COMMIT"

sections.title: Scoping is where ARG surprises people
paragraphs: ARG is the only instruction allowed before FROM, which is how you parameterise the base image:
Omit that second declaration and $NODE_VERSION expands to nothing, with no warning:
The same rule applies to every stage of a multi-stage build:

codeBlock.code:
ARG NODE_VERSION=22
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-alpine

# The pre-FROM ARG is out of scope here, re-declare to use it
ARG NODE_VERSION
RUN echo "Running on Node $NODE_VERSION"

sections.title: Promoting ARG to ENV
paragraphs: The standard pattern when a build-time value must also exist at runtime:

Do this only for things that are safe to publish: a version string, a build date, a commit SHA. Promoting a token to ENV takes something already in the build history and makes it visible in docker inspect too.

You want to build an image tagged myapp:3.0.0, passing a build argument APP_VERSION=3.0.0 (which the Dockerfile promotes from ARG to ENV). Then you want to run the container and print the value of APP_VERSION from inside it. Which sequence of commands is correct?

codeBlock.code:
ARG APP_VERSION=1.0.0
ENV APP_VERSION=${APP_VERSION}

sections.title: Why ARG is not safe for secrets
paragraphs: This looks careful. The file is deleted in the same layer:
But the value was passed as a build argument, and build arguments are recorded:
Anyone who can pull the image can read that. Rotating the token is the only remedy once an image has shipped.
The fix is a BuildKit secret mount, which makes the value available to one instruction and writes it to no layer:

codeBlock.code:
ARG NPM_TOKEN
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc \
 && npm ci \
 && rm .npmrc

sections.title: ARG and the build cache
paragraphs: An ARG invalidates the cache from the point it is first used, not from where it is declared. Declaring ten build args and using one changes nothing about the other nine.
That makes it a precise cache-busting tool:
Everything above that line stays cached; everything from it rebuilds.

codeBlock.code:
ARG CACHE_BUST=1
RUN apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y

sections.title: Predefined build arguments
paragraphs: Some args exist without being declared. The platform ones are what make cross-compilation work:
The build stage runs natively on the builder and cross-compiles to the target, which avoids emulation entirely and is what stops an arm64 build producing an exec format error on amd64 servers.
HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY are also predefined and, usefully, are excluded from docker history.

codeBlock.code:
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.23 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/server .

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile declares ARG NODE_VERSION=22 before FROM, uses it successfully in the FROM line, then RUN echo "Node $NODE_VERSION" prints "Node" with no number. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between ARG and ENV in a Dockerfile?

ARG defines a variable that exists only while docker build runs and is gone once the image is finished. Nothing inside a running container can see it. ENV writes a variable into the image so it is present during the remainder of the build and in every container started from that image. Use ARG for things that shape how the image is built, such as a base image version or a commit SHA, and ENV for configuration the application reads at runtime, such as a port or log level.
Is it safe to pass a secret with --build-arg?

No. The value is recorded in the image's build metadata and docker history --no-trunc prints it back, even if the file you wrote it to was deleted in the same RUN. Anyone who can pull the image can recover it, and rotating the credential is the only fix after the fact. Use a BuildKit secret mount instead, RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token … with docker build --secret id=token,env=TOKEN, which exposes the value to a single instruction and writes it to no layer.
Why is my ARG empty after FROM?

Because the region before the first FROM is a separate scope, and build stages do not inherit from it. That scope exists so the base image itself can be parameterised. Add a bare ARG NODE_VERSION after FROM to bring the value into that stage, and repeat it in every stage of a multi-stage build that needs it. Docker gives no warning. An out-of-scope variable simply expands to an empty string.
How do I override an environment variable at runtime?

docker run -e LOG_LEVEL=debug myapp overrides whatever the Dockerfile's ENV set, with no rebuild. In Compose, use environment: for inline values or env_file: for a file. Precedence runs from most to least specific: docker run -e beats Compose environment:, which beats env_file:, which beats the Dockerfile's ENV. Treat ENV as the image's default rather than a fixed value.
Why does changing --build-arg rebuild my whole image?

It does not rebuild the whole image. It invalidates the cache from the point the argument is first used, and everything above stays cached. If that feels like everything, the ARG is probably referenced earlier than it needs to be, often in a FROM line or an early RUN. Moving its first use further down keeps the expensive install layers cached. The same behaviour is useful deliberately: ARG CACHE_BUST placed just above an apt-get upgrade forces exactly that step to re-run.
Should I use ENV or a .env file for configuration?

Different tools for different jobs. Dockerfile ENV bakes a default into the image, which is right for values that are part of the image itself: a PATH addition, PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, a default port. A .env file is read by Docker Compose on your machine and never enters the image, which makes it right for per-environment values and for anything you would not publish. In production the orchestrator supplies the values, typically from a Kubernetes Secret or a parameter store, and the image's ENV defaults just fill the gaps.

quickReference.command: docker run --rm myapp env | grep NODE_ENV

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn what WORKDIR, EXPOSE, USER, LABEL and HEALTHCHECK do in a Dockerfile, why EXPOSE publishes nothing, and when VOLUME causes problems in builds.

These are the instructions that turn a Dockerfile that builds into one you would put in production. Two of them do considerably less than their names suggest, which is where most of the confusion lives.

sections.title: WORKDIR
paragraphs: WORKDIR sets the directory for every RUN, COPY, ADD, CMD and ENTRYPOINT that follows, and it is where you land when you docker exec into the container.
It creates the directory if it does not exist, so RUN mkdir -p /app before it is redundant.
Each RUN starts a fresh shell, so a cd inside one has no effect on the next. This is a common source of files landing in / when the author was certain they were in /app.
Relative WORKDIR stacks, which works until someone inserts a WORKDIR above it.
WORKDIR creates directories owned by root, even when a USER instruction came earlier:
Create and chown the directory before dropping privileges:

codeBlock.code:
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json .        # → /app/package.json
RUN npm ci                 # runs in /app
CMD ["node", "server.js"]  # runs /app/server.js

sections.title: EXPOSE publishes nothing
paragraphs: This is the single most misunderstood instruction in Docker.
EXPOSE is metadata. It opens no port, maps nothing, and changes no networking behaviour. A container with EXPOSE 3000 is not reachable from your host:
Publishing is a runtime decision:
Equally: a container without EXPOSE is still reachable by other containers on the same Docker network, and still publishable with -p. The instruction genuinely changes nothing about connectivity.

So why write it? Three real reasons: it documents the interface for whoever runs the image, docker run -P uses it to auto-publish every exposed port to a random host port, and Compose and other tooling read it when wiring services.
If a published port still refuses connections, the usual cause is the application binding to 127.0.0.1 inside the container rather than 0.0.0.0. Localhost inside a container is that container alone.

codeBlock.code:
EXPOSE 3000          # TCP by default
EXPOSE 8080/tcp
EXPOSE 53/udp
EXPOSE 80 443

sections.title: USER
paragraphs: Containers run as root by default. That is unnecessary for nearly every application and materially worse when combined with a mounted host path.
Many official images already ship a non-root user: node, nginx, postgres. For your own:
Place USER after anything that needs root, and step back up briefly when you must:
Kubernetes' runAsNonRoot: true check runs before the image's user database is consulted, so a named user cannot be verified and the Pod fails to start:
A numeric USER avoids it. USER 1000:1000 sets the group too.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .

USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: LABEL
paragraphs: Key-value metadata, visible in docker inspect and filterable with docker images --filter.

Use the OCI standard keys rather than inventing your own. Tooling reads them, and org.opencontainers.image.source in particular is what makes GitHub link a published package back to its repository automatically.
Combine labels into one instruction; each LABEL is a layer.

codeBlock.code:
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"

sections.title: VOLUME is usually a mistake
paragraphs: This declares that a path should be backed by a volume, and Docker creates an anonymous volume for it whenever the container starts without an explicit -v.
That sounds helpful and mostly is not:

Declare the path in your documentation and let docker run -v or a Compose volumes: entry do the work. VOLUME earns its place mainly in database images, where accidentally running without persistence is the worse failure.

codeBlock.code: VOLUME /app/data

sections.title: HEALTHCHECK
paragraphs: --start-period is the one that matters most. Without enough of it, a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

Worth being blunt about, because it is widely assumed otherwise: Kubernetes does not read a Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK. It uses its own livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe, and an image's healthcheck has no effect on scheduling, restarts or traffic routing.
HEALTHCHECK is useful for plain docker run, Docker Compose (depends_on with condition: service_healthy) and Docker Swarm. On Kubernetes, define probes in the Pod spec instead:

You are completing a Dockerfile based on node:20-alpine. After installing dependencies and copying the source (owned by node:node), you need to: document that the app listens on port 3000, switch to the non-root "node" user, and start the app with "node server.js" using exec form. Which set of instructions, in order, is correct?

codeBlock.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Dockerfile declares VOLUME /app/data and then, on a later line, COPY seed.json /app/data/. The build succeeds, but /app/data is empty in every container. Why?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Does EXPOSE actually open a port in Docker?

No. EXPOSE records which port the containerised application listens on, for people reading the Dockerfile and for tooling. Nothing more. It opens nothing, maps nothing, and a container without it is just as reachable. To reach the application from your host you need -p 8080:3000 at docker run, and containers on the same Docker network can reach each other regardless. The one functional use is docker run -P, which publishes every exposed port to a random host port.
Why can't I reach my container even though I used -p?

Almost always because the application is bound to 127.0.0.1 inside the container. Localhost inside a container refers to that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Configure the server to bind 0.0.0.0, in Express that is app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0'), in Flask --host=0.0.0.0. Confirm what is actually listening with docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp before changing anything else.
Why does my container get "permission denied" after I added USER?

Usually because a directory was created after the USER instruction. WORKDIR creates directories owned by root regardless of the current user, so USER node followed by WORKDIR /app/cache leaves the application unable to write to its own cache. Create and chown the directory while still root, then drop privileges. The other common cause is copied files still owned by root, which COPY --chown=node:node fixes in the same layer.
Should I use VOLUME in my Dockerfile?

Usually not, for application images. It creates an anonymous volume on every run that omits -v, and those pile up on the host until someone prunes them. Worse, any COPY or RUN writing to that path after the declaration is masked at runtime by the mount, so seed data silently disappears. Let whoever runs the container decide with -v or a Compose volumes: entry. It is defensible in database images, where the greater risk is someone running without persistence at all.
Does Kubernetes use the Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK?

No, and this trips up a lot of teams. Kubernetes ignores the image's HEALTHCHECK completely and relies on livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe defined in the Pod spec. An image with a perfect healthcheck gets no scheduling, restart or traffic-routing benefit on Kubernetes. HEALTHCHECK remains useful for plain docker run, for Docker Swarm, and for Compose's depends_on with condition: service_healthy.
What is the difference between WORKDIR and RUN cd?

RUN cd /app changes directory inside the shell that runs that one instruction, and that shell exits immediately afterwards, so the next instruction starts back at the previous directory. WORKDIR /app sets the directory for every subsequent instruction, persists into the final image as the container's starting directory, and creates the path if it does not exist. Use WORKDIR; the only place cd makes sense is chained within a single RUN, as in RUN cd /src && make install.
