sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Write safer, smaller Dockerfiles. Covers exec form for SIGTERM, non-root users, secrets, layer order, multi-stage builds, pinned bases, scanning and hadolint.

A Dockerfile that builds is not the same as one you would put in production. These are the practices that matter, ordered by what they actually buy you, because a checklist where every item looks equally important is a checklist nobody finishes.
The top five below cover most of the real-world damage. The rest are worth doing and none of them will page you at 3am.

sections.title: 1. Exec form, or your app never gets SIGTERM
paragraphs: The most commonly shipped Dockerfile bug, because everything looks fine until a deploy.

Shell form becomes /bin/sh -c "node server.js". The shell is PID 1; your application is its child. When Docker or Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, sh receives it and does not forward it. Your app keeps serving until the grace period expires and SIGKILL arrives. Dropping in-flight requests on every single deploy.
Exec form makes your process PID 1 and it receives the signal directly.

A second, subtler catch: the kernel gives PID 1 no default action for SIGTERM. A process that never installs a handler ignores it even in exec form. Most frameworks handle this; plenty of scripts do not.
If your application cannot handle signals, or spawns children that leave zombies, give it a real init:
Some servers want a different signal entirely:

codeBlock.code:
CMD node server.js            # shell form
CMD ["node", "server.js"]     # exec form

sections.title: 2. Never run as root
paragraphs: Root in a container is not root on the host in the way it once was, but it removes a layer of defence for free, and combined with a mounted host path or a kernel vulnerability it is the difference between an incident and a catastrophe.
Use a numeric UID if the image will run on Kubernetes, runAsNonRoot: true cannot verify a named user and the Pod fails to start.
Then take the next step and make the filesystem read-only:
An attacker who cannot write to the filesystem cannot drop a payload on it.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --chown=node:node . .
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: 3. Secrets never survive deletion
paragraphs: Deleting the file afterwards changes nothing. Layers are immutable, and the deletion only adds a whiteout on top.
Use a secret mount, which exists for one instruction and is written to no layer:
Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotating it is the only remedy.

codeBlock.code:
ENV DB_PASSWORD=supersecret          # in docker inspect, forever
ARG NPM_TOKEN                        # in docker history, forever

sections.title: 4. Order layers by change frequency
paragraphs: Docker reuses cached layers up to the first changed instruction, then rebuilds everything below. COPY . . above the install means every one-character edit reinstalls every dependency.
Add cache mounts for the step itself, which keeps the package cache on the builder without putting a byte in the image:
And write .dockerignore before your first COPY . .:
Three benefits at once: a smaller build context, no cache invalidation from irrelevant files, and local secrets that never reach a layer.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine              # changes on version bumps
WORKDIR /app
RUN apk add --no-cache curl      # changes rarely

COPY package*.json ./            # changes when dependencies do
RUN npm ci --omit=dev            # expensive. Keep it cached

COPY . .                         # changes every commit
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

sections.title: 5. Multi-stage builds
paragraphs: Compilers, dev dependencies and source never reach what ships. For Go and Rust the effect is order-of-magnitude. A few hundred megabytes of build environment becomes a binary in a scratch or distroless/static image.
It is a security practice as much as a size one. A compiler in a production image is a tool an attacker gets for free.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER 1000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: 6. Pin the base image
paragraphs: Pin a digest and let Renovate or Dependabot bump it, so updates arrive as reviewable pull requests. Where you keep a tag, rebuild with --pull so a stale cached base does not quietly carry old CVEs into a "fresh" build.

codeBlock.code:
FROM node:latest                      # moves without warning
FROM node:22.11.0-alpine3.20          # a specific release
FROM node:22-alpine@sha256:bf77dc26…  # immutable

sections.title: 7. Scan, and fail the build on it
paragraphs: That exit code is the part that matters. A scan whose output nobody reads is theatre; a scan that fails the pipeline is a control. Start with CRITICAL only if the backlog is large, then tighten.
Generate provenance and an SBOM while you are there. Increasingly expected, and one flag each:

codeBlock.code:
docker scout cves myapp:1.0
trivy image myapp:1.0

sections.title: 8. Lint it
paragraphs: Hadolint catches most of this list mechanically:

codeBlock.code: docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile

sections.title: 9. Health checks, with one caveat
paragraphs: --start-period is the option that matters. Too little and a slow-starting application is marked unhealthy while it is still booting.

Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK entirely. It reads only livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe from the Pod spec. The instruction is genuinely useful for docker run, Swarm, and Compose's depends_on: condition: service_healthy, just do not expect it to do anything on a cluster.

codeBlock.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=40s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

sections.title: 10. Label for provenance
paragraphs: image.source is the one that earns its keep: it is what lets a registry link a published image back to the repository that built it, and what lets an on-call engineer find the code from a running container at 3am.
You want to run hadolint against the Dockerfile in the current directory using the official hadolint Docker image, without leaving behind a stopped container afterward. Which command is correct?

codeBlock.code:
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/repo" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="$GIT_SHA" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="2.1.0" \
      org.opencontainers.image.licenses="MIT"

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: Every rolling deploy drops in-flight requests. The container takes the full termination grace period and is then killed. The Dockerfile ends with CMD node server.js and the app does handle SIGTERM. What is wrong?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why doesn't my container stop gracefully on docker stop?

Almost certainly shell-form CMD. Written as CMD node server.js, Docker runs /bin/sh -c "node server.js", making the shell PID 1 and your application its child, and sh receives SIGTERM without forwarding it. After the grace period Docker sends SIGKILL and everything in flight is lost. Use exec form: CMD ["node", "server.js"]. If the process genuinely cannot handle signals, run with --init or add tini as the entrypoint.
Is it really a problem to run a container as root?

It is a defence you are giving up for one line. Container isolation is good, so root inside a container is not automatically root on the host, but combined with a bind-mounted host path, a privileged flag, or a kernel vulnerability, the gap closes fast. Add USER 1000, and on Kubernetes pair it with runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and dropped capabilities. Use a numeric UID, because runAsNonRoot cannot verify a named user and the Pod will refuse to start.
How do I pass a secret to a Docker build safely?

With a BuildKit secret mount. RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token … makes the value readable at /run/secrets/npm_token for that one instruction and writes it to no layer, with docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN supplying it. Do not use ARG or ENV: both are recorded in the image metadata and docker history --no-trunc prints them back, even when the file you wrote was deleted in the same RUN. Once a secret has shipped in an image, rotation is the only fix.
What is the fastest way to make my Docker image smaller?

In order: use a multi-stage build so compilers and dev dependencies never ship, switch to a -slim or -alpine base variant (but not Alpine for Python), and make sure every cleanup happens in the same RUN as the thing it cleans up. Run docker history <image> --no-trunc first. It names the instruction responsible for each layer's size, which usually makes the answer obvious and saves you optimising something that was never the problem.
Which Dockerfile linter should I use, and what should it fail on?

Hadolint is the standard, and it runs as a container so there is nothing to install: docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile. In CI, set failure-threshold: warning. Its defaults are sensible and most of its rules map to genuine production problems, such as DL3002 for a root final user and DL3025 for shell-form CMD. Pair it with an image scanner such as Trivy or Docker Scout, and give that a non-zero exit code on HIGH and CRITICAL so results block a merge rather than scroll past in a log.
Do I need a HEALTHCHECK in my Dockerfile?

Only if something reads it. docker run, Docker Swarm and Compose's depends_on: condition: service_healthy all do, and it is worth adding there. Kubernetes does not. It uses livenessProbe, readinessProbe and startupProbe from the Pod spec and ignores the image's healthcheck completely, so on a cluster the instruction buys you nothing and the probes are what you need to get right. Wherever you do use it, set --start-period generously or slow-starting applications are marked unhealthy while still booting.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Copy production-ready Dockerfile examples for Node.js, Python FastAPI, Go, React with Nginx, Spring Boot and Django, and see the pattern they all share.

Complete, production-shaped Dockerfiles you can adapt. Every one of them follows the same five-part skeleton. Build stage, minimal runtime stage, manifests cached before source, non-root user, exec-form start command, and each section calls out the specific mistake that shape avoids.

sections.title: Node.js API (TypeScript)
paragraphs: The TypeScript compiler and every dev dependency stay in the build stage. The runtime stage installs production dependencies fresh rather than copying node_modules across. Copying them would bring the dev tree with it, which is the usual reason a "multi-stage" Node image is no smaller than a single-stage one.
COPY --chown rather than a trailing RUN chown -R: the latter rewrites every file into a new layer.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ── Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json tsconfig.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build                      # → /app/dist

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app

ENV NODE_ENV=production

COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

COPY --from=build --chown=node:node /app/dist ./dist

LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/org/api"

USER node
EXPOSE 3000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

sections.title: Python FastAPI
paragraphs: Three details doing real work here.
-slim, not -alpine. PyPI's prebuilt wheels target glibc, so Alpine forces pip to compile nearly everything from source. Slower builds and frequently a larger image.
libpq-dev in the build stage, libpq5 at runtime. The -dev package carries headers and a compiler toolchain that the running application has no use for.
--host 0.0.0.0. Uvicorn defaults to 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means that container only. This is the single most common cause of a published port that still refuses connections.
PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 matters more than it looks: without it, Python buffers stdout and your logs arrive in chunks, or not at all when the container is killed.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ── Build wheels ───────────────────────────────────────
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc libpq-dev \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 appuser && chown appuser /app

COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . .
USER 1000
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "4"]

sections.title: Go (static binary on scratch)
paragraphs: CGO_ENABLED=0 is not optional. A dynamically linked binary in scratch dies instantly with no such file or directory. The missing file being the dynamic linker, which is why the message names nothing helpful.
scratch has no CA certificates and no timezone database, so any HTTPS call fails and every timestamp is UTC until you copy both across.
-ldflags="-w -s" strips the symbol table and DWARF debug info, typically cutting the binary by around a quarter.

The $BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETARCH combination cross-compiles natively on the builder rather than running the whole build under emulation, which is both much faster and what prevents an exec format error when an arm64 Mac builds for amd64 servers.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.23-alpine AS build
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates tzdata

WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download

COPY . .
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH \
    go build -ldflags="-w -s" -o /out/server .

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/
COPY --from=build /usr/share/zoneinfo /usr/share/zoneinfo
COPY --from=build /out/server /server

EXPOSE 8080
USER 1000
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

sections.title: React SPA behind Nginx
paragraphs: STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT is the detail most nginx images miss. Nginx treats SIGTERM as a fast shutdown that cuts active connections, and SIGQUIT as a graceful drain. Without this line every deploy severs in-flight requests.

Build args are baked in, not configurable at runtime. VITE_API_URL is compiled into the JavaScript bundle, so one image cannot serve two environments. If you need that, serve a small /config.json that the app fetches at startup instead.

codeBlock.code:
# ── Build ──────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
ARG VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
ENV VITE_API_URL=${VITE_API_URL}
RUN npm run build                      # → /app/dist

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
RUN rm /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/app.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

EXPOSE 80
STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT
CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]

sections.title: Spring Boot (layered JAR)
paragraphs: JRE at runtime, JDK only to build. Shipping the JDK adds a compiler and hundreds of megabytes for no benefit.

layertools extract splits the fat JAR into layers that change at different rates. Dependencies rarely change and stay cached; your application classes are the last, tiny layer. Copying the whole JAR instead means every one-line code change re-pushes the entire thing.

codeBlock.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw pom.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 ./mvnw dependency:go-offline

COPY src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 ./mvnw package -DskipTests
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract --destination extracted

# ── Runtime ────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S -u 1000 -G spring spring

COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=spring:spring /app/extracted/application/ ./

USER 1000
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

sections.title: Django + Gunicorn
paragraphs: collectstatic runs at build time so the image is self-contained and container start stays fast. Note it needs settings that do not require a database connection. A DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE pointing at build-safe settings is the usual arrangement.
A Node.js Dockerfile builds in one stage and then copies both /app/dist and /app/node_modules from it into the runtime stage. The final image is the same size as the old single-stage one. Why?

codeBlock.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim

ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 django && chown django /app

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt

COPY --chown=django:django . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

USER 1000
EXPOSE 8000

CMD ["gunicorn", "myproject.wsgi:application", \
     "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", \
     "--workers", "4", \
     "--timeout", "120"]

paragraphs: To adapt one: change the base image to your pinned version, point the start command at your entry file, bind to 0.0.0.0 rather than localhost, and check whether your runtime needs a system library that only appeared in the build stage.
An Nginx container serving a React SPA severs in-flight requests each time it is replaced, even though the app is static and the rollout is gradual. Which Dockerfile line fixes it?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does a production-ready Dockerfile look like?

Five things, in every language: a build stage holding the compiler and dev dependencies, a runtime stage on the smallest base that can run the output, dependency manifests copied and installed before source so the expensive layer stays cached, a non-root numeric USER with ownership set via COPY --chown, and an exec-form CMD so the process receives SIGTERM. Add EXPOSE, OCI labels and a health check for tooling. Anything beyond that is tuning.
Why is my multi-stage Node.js image still large?

Almost certainly because node_modules is being copied from the build stage. That directory was produced by npm ci, which installs devDependencies alongside production ones because the TypeScript compiler needs them, so copying it forward brings the entire dev tree into production. Copy only the build output, and run npm ci --omit=dev separately in the runtime stage. Copying package*.json first there keeps that install cached too.
Should I use Alpine or slim for a Python Dockerfile?

-slim, in nearly every case. Alpine uses musl, and PyPI's prebuilt manylinux wheels target glibc, so pip install falls back to compiling from source. That turns a twenty-second install into several minutes, requires gcc and development headers in the image, and often produces a larger result than the slim variant. Alpine is an excellent choice for Go and Rust; for Python it usually costs on every axis you were trying to optimise.
How do I pass environment-specific configuration to a React Docker image?

A build arg such as VITE_API_URL is compiled into the JavaScript bundle, which means one image per environment and a rebuild for every change. Fine if your pipeline builds per environment anyway. If you want a single image promoted from staging to production, serve a small /config.json that Nginx can have mounted or generated at container start, and have the app fetch it before rendering. Runtime environment variables cannot reach an already-built bundle.
Why does my containerised app work locally but refuse connections in Docker?

The server is bound to 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means that container alone, so Docker's port mapping delivers traffic to an interface nothing is listening on. Bind 0.0.0.0 instead: --host 0.0.0.0 for Uvicorn, --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 for Gunicorn, app.listen(3000, '0.0.0.0') in Express. Confirm with docker exec <container> netstat -tlnp, which shows what is actually listening and on which address.
Why does my Go container exit immediately with "no such file or directory"?

The binary is dynamically linked and the file the kernel cannot find is the dynamic linker, not your program, which is why the error names nothing useful. Build with CGO_ENABLED=0 to produce a fully static binary. While you are there, remember that scratch also lacks TLS root certificates and timezone data, so copy /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt and /usr/share/zoneinfo from the build stage, or use gcr.io/distroless/static, which ships both.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn why container data disappears and how Docker volumes fix it. Compare the three mount types, handle permission problems, and back up or clean up volumes.
Anything a container writes to its own filesystem is destroyed when the container is removed. Volumes are how data outlives the container that created it.
This catches essentially everyone once. A database container is recreated, and the data is gone.

sections.title: Why container data disappears
paragraphs: A container has a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image layers. It exists for the life of that container and is deleted with it.

Note that docker stop and docker start preserve the writable layer, only docker rm destroys it. But since replacing containers is the normal way to deploy a new image, anything valuable must live outside.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d --name db postgres:17
# ... write some data ...
docker rm -f db
docker run -d --name db postgres:17      # empty. The data was in the old writable layer.

sections.title: The three mount types
paragraphs: The modern --mount syntax is more explicit and worth preferring in scripts, since -v silently creates a directory when a host path does not exist rather than erroring:

codeBlock.code:
# Named volume
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

# Bind mount
docker run -d -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src myapp:dev

# tmpfs
docker run -d --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m myapp

sections.title: Named volumes
paragraphs: Docker manages the location, the lifecycle and the permissions:
They live under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux and inside the Docker Desktop VM on macOS and Windows, which is deliberate, because not caring where they live is the point.
To look inside one without a running container:
Use named volumes for application data. They are portable between hosts, behave identically across platforms, and perform far better than bind mounts on macOS and Windows.

codeBlock.code:
docker volume create pgdata
docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata

sections.title: Bind mounts
paragraphs: A direct mapping of a host path into the container:

The standard development pattern: mount your source so edits appear instantly, and use that second anonymous volume to shadow node_modules. Otherwise the host's empty or platform-mismatched directory hides the one installed during the build.

They are slow on macOS and Windows. Every file access crosses into the Docker VM, which is painful for projects with many small files. Mount only what you need, keep dependency directories in named volumes, and enable VirtioFS in Docker Desktop.
Mount read-only where you can:

codeBlock.code: docker run -d -v $(pwd):/app -v /app/node_modules myapp:dev

sections.title: The permissions problem
paragraphs: On Linux, a container running as root writes files owned by root onto your host:
The container preserves real UIDs rather than remapping them. Fix it by running as your own user:
The reverse also happens: a container running as a non-root user cannot write to a host directory owned by you, producing permission denied. Matching the UID is the reliable fix.
This is Linux-specific. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows handles the mapping.
For named volumes Docker sets ownership from the image's declared user on first use, which is why they largely avoid this class of problem.

codeBlock.code:
$ ls -l output/
-rw-r--r-- 1 root root  1024 Sep 16 10:00 report.csv

sections.title: Backing up
paragraphs: There is no built-in backup command. The pattern is a throwaway container mounting both the volume and a host directory:
For a database, prefer the engine's own dump tool. Copying live database files can capture a torn, inconsistent state:

codeBlock.code:
# Back up
docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/pgdata-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data .

# Restore
docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
  tar xzf /backup/pgdata-2026-09-16.tar.gz -C /data

sections.title: Reclaiming space
paragraphs: Volumes are excluded from docker system prune by default, deliberately, because they hold the data you least want to lose:

The hidden consumer is anonymous volumes. An image declaring VOLUME /data creates a fresh unnamed volume on every docker run if you do not mount one there, so repeatedly starting a database image leaves a trail of orphaned volumes holding real data.
Avoid them by always mounting a named volume explicitly, and by using --rm, which removes anonymous volumes on exit.

codeBlock.code:
docker system df -v          # usage per volume
docker volume prune          # remove volumes no container references
docker system prune --volumes   # include them in a general clean

sections.title: Key takeaways
paragraphs: A Postgres container is recreated after an image update and all data is gone. It was started with docker run -d postgres:17 and no volume. What happened?
A server is short on disk. docker system prune -a frees some space but docker volume ls still shows dozens of volumes. Why were they not removed?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Why does my Docker container lose data when it restarts?

It does not lose data on restart, docker stop and docker start preserve the container's writable layer. Data is lost when the container is removed, which is what happens when you deploy a new image or run docker rm. Since replacing containers is the normal deployment model, anything valuable must live in a volume mounted into the container rather than in its own filesystem.
What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?

A named volume is managed by Docker, referenced by name, and stored somewhere Docker chooses. A bind mount maps a specific host directory into the container. Use named volumes for persistent application data. They are portable across hosts, handle permissions better, and are considerably faster on macOS and Windows. Use bind mounts for development, where you want host edits reflected in the container immediately, and for mounting host configuration read-only.
How do I fix "permission denied" on a Docker volume?

On Linux, the container preserves real user IDs rather than remapping them, so a container running as a non-root user cannot write to a host directory owned by you, and a root container creates root-owned files on your host. Run the container as your own user with docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g), or set a matching USER in the Dockerfile. Named volumes largely avoid this because Docker sets ownership from the image's declared user on first use.
How do I back up a Docker volume?

Use a throwaway container that mounts both the volume and a host directory, then archive one into the other: docker run --rm -v myvol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tar.gz -C /data .. There is no built-in backup command. For databases, use the engine's own dump tool instead, pg_dump, mysqldump, because copying live database files can capture an inconsistent state that will not restore cleanly.
Why didn't docker system prune free up my volume space?

Because volumes are excluded by default, deliberately, since they usually contain the data you would least want removed by a routine cleanup. Use docker volume prune to remove volumes no container references, or docker system prune --volumes to include them. Check docker system df -v first to see which volumes are actually consuming space, and be aware the deletion is permanent.
What are anonymous volumes and why do I keep getting them?

When an image declares VOLUME /data in its Dockerfile and you run it without mounting anything at that path, Docker creates an unnamed volume with a random hexadecimal ID. Every docker run creates another, so repeatedly starting a database image leaves a trail of orphaned volumes each holding real data. Always mount a named volume explicitly at the documented path, and add --rm to one-off runs, which removes anonymous volumes when the container exits.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Create Docker named volumes with docker volume create, -v and --mount. See how data survives container removal and how to share a volume.

A container is easy to replace. That is one of Docker’s biggest strengths. But the same feature creates a serious problem the moment your application stores real data. If you remove a container that has been writing into its own filesystem, that data disappears with it. Named volumes solve this by moving important data outside the container lifecycle.
Named volumes are the standard Docker answer for persistent application storage. They are simple to use, portable across containers, and managed directly by Docker.

sections.title: What Are Named Volumes?
paragraphs: A named volume is a Docker-managed storage location with a name you choose, such as postgres-data or uploads. Instead of mounting a host path manually, you tell Docker to attach that volume name to a container path.
Named volumes are useful because they separate data lifecycle from container lifecycle.
A container may be stopped, replaced, recreated, or upgraded. The volume remains until you explicitly remove it.
That makes named volumes ideal for:

codeBlock.code: docker run -d --name db -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

Docker responds with the volume name:
Now it exists independently of any container.
Explicit creation helps because you can:
Descriptive names make cleanup and troubleshooting much easier later.

sections.title: Mounting Volumes with -v
paragraphs: The shortest syntax is -v.
Docker checks whether myvolume exists:
If the app writes files into /app/data, those files stay in the volume even if you remove the container.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  --name app \
  -v myvolume:/app/data \
  my-image

sections.title: Mounting Volumes with --mount
paragraphs: The --mount syntax is longer but clearer and more explicit.
This says the same thing as the -v example, but the fields are named:
--mount is easier to read in scripts and documentation, especially once you add more options. With -v, beginners sometimes mix up volume names and host paths. --mount makes the intent explicit.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  --name app \
  --mount type=volume,source=myvolume,target=/app/data \
  my-image

sections.title: Understanding docker run -v myvolume:/app/data
paragraphs: This command is worth pausing on because it is one of the most important volume patterns in Docker.
The key insight is that the container path acts like an attachment point. The real data is not tied to the container filesystem anymore.

codeBlock.code: docker run -v myvolume:/app/data my-image

sections.title: Persistence Across Container Removal
paragraphs: Named volumes become most valuable when you replace containers.
The database files remain because they live in pgdata, not in the removed container.
This pattern is extremely common in upgrades:

codeBlock.code:
# First container writes data
docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

# Later, remove the container
docker rm -f db

# Recreate a fresh container with the same volume
docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

sections.title: Sharing a Volume Between Multiple Containers
paragraphs: One named volume can be mounted into more than one container.
The safest design is usually:

If multiple containers write to the same files without coordination, data corruption can happen. The volume itself does not provide application-level locking. Your application still needs to handle concurrency correctly.

codeBlock.code:
docker volume create shared-data

docker run -d \
  --name writer \
  -v shared-data:/data \
  alpine sh -c "while true; do date >> /data/log.txt; sleep 5; done"

docker run -d \
  --name reader \
  -v shared-data:/logs:ro \
  alpine sh -c "tail -f /logs/log.txt"

sections.title: Inspecting Volumes with docker volume ls

If your machine has many projects, docker volume ls becomes a routine cleanup and troubleshooting command.

codeBlock.code: docker volume ls

sections.title: Inspecting Details with docker volume inspect

sections.title: Where Docker Stores Volume Data on the Host
paragraphs: On Linux with the local driver, Docker often stores named volume data under a path like:

On Docker Desktop for macOS and Windows, Docker usually runs inside a lightweight VM. That means the volume data is not as directly accessible in the same way as on a native Linux host. You should think of Docker as managing the location for you rather than relying on browsing the files manually.
That is one reason named volumes are nice: your workflow does not depend heavily on knowing the exact host path.

codeBlock.code: /var/lib/docker/volumes/<volume-name>/_data

sections.title: Volume Drivers
paragraphs: The default volume driver is local, and that is what most beginners use.
This uses the local driver unless you specify something else.
The local driver stores volume data on the same Docker host. It is perfect for:

sections.title: Removing Volumes with docker volume rm
paragraphs: To delete a specific volume:
Docker removes the volume only if it is not in use by a container.
If a container still references the volume, Docker refuses:
That safety check helps prevent accidental data loss.
Before removing a volume, make sure:

sections.title: Cleaning Up with docker volume prune
paragraphs: Over time, volumes accumulate. Some are still important. Others are leftovers from experiments, deleted containers, or old Compose projects.
To remove all unused volumes:
Docker asks for confirmation. To skip the prompt:

An “unused” volume may still contain important data. Docker only knows whether a volume is attached to a container, not whether you care about the contents. Always inspect before pruning in environments that matter.

codeBlock.code: docker volume prune

sections.title: Named Volumes vs Bind Mounts
paragraphs: Named volumes and bind mounts both store data outside the container, but they serve different needs.
If you are storing database files, named volumes are usually the right first choice.

sections.title: Practical Use Cases
paragraphs: These examples all share one theme: the data should persist even if the container changes.

codeBlock.code: docker run -d --name postgres -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

sections.title: Best Practices
paragraphs: Prefer postgres-data over data1. Clear names reduce mistakes.
A named volume is persistent, but it is not magical. You can still delete it. Persistence is not the same as backup.
Let Docker and your containers manage the data unless you have a specific reason to intervene.
A volume does not protect you from concurrent write issues.
Unused volumes quietly consume disk space. Periodic inspection and pruning keep your host healthy.

sections.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: Assuming deleting a container deletes the volume It does not. Named volumes persist independently.
Using bind mounts for database data without a reason This often adds host-path complexity you do not need.
Removing a volume before checking its contents That can destroy important application state.
Forgetting that Docker can auto-create volumes This can lead to accidental anonymous or unexpected volumes if you mistype a name.
Expecting a volume to solve application-level file locking It only provides shared storage, not concurrency control.

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: Named volumes are the default Docker answer for persistent container data. They are simple, reliable, and designed for the exact problem containers create: disposable compute with durable storage. Learn the docker volume create, docker volume ls, docker volume inspect, and docker volume rm commands well, and you will be comfortable managing stateful Docker workloads.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Docker named volume?

A storage area managed by Docker, referenced by a name rather than a host path. Docker decides where it physically lives, under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ on Linux, and handles its lifecycle. Named volumes are the recommended way to persist container data because they are portable across hosts, work identically on Linux, macOS and Windows, and can be backed up, inspected and managed with docker volume commands.
What is the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?

A named volume is managed by Docker and referenced by name; a bind mount maps a specific host directory into the container. Named volumes are better for persistent application data, a database's files, uploaded content, because they are portable and Docker manages permissions and location. Bind mounts are better for development, where you want to edit files on the host and see changes inside the container immediately. Bind mounts are also noticeably slower on macOS and Windows.
Where are Docker named volumes stored?

On Linux, under /var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data. On macOS and Windows they live inside the Linux VM that Docker Desktop manages, so the path is not directly browsable from the host, which is deliberate, since the point of a named volume is that you do not manage its location. Use docker volume inspect <name> to see the mountpoint, and docker run --rm -v <name>:/data alpine ls /data to look inside.
Do named volumes survive container deletion?

Yes. That is their purpose. Removing a container leaves its named volumes intact, so recreating the container reattaches the same data. This also means they accumulate: docker container prune does not remove them, and neither does plain docker system prune without the --volumes flag. Run docker volume ls periodically, and docker volume prune to remove volumes no container references.
How do I back up a Docker volume?

Run a throwaway container that mounts both the volume and a host directory, then archive one into the other: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data .. Restoring reverses it. For a database, prefer the engine's own dump tool over a filesystem copy, since copying live database files can capture an inconsistent state.
Can multiple containers share a named volume?

Yes, and it is a common pattern. One container writes files and another reads them, or several replicas share a cache. Mount the same volume name in each. Be aware Docker provides no coordination: if two containers write to the same files concurrently you are responsible for avoiding corruption, exactly as you would be with two processes on a host. Most databases explicitly do not support multiple instances sharing one data directory.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Learn how to use a Docker bind mount with -v and --mount to share a host directory, make it read-only with :ro, and set up live reload for development.

Bind mounts are one of the most practical Docker features for local development. They let a container see files that already exist on your host machine, and they let the host see changes made by the container. That direct connection is powerful, fast, and sometimes dangerous, which is why you need to understand it clearly.
If named volumes are the best default for persistent application data, bind mounts are often the best default for source code, configuration files, and developer workflows.

sections.title: What Are Bind Mounts?
paragraphs: A bind mount maps a specific path on the host into a path inside a container.
The container is not using Docker-managed storage in this case. It is reading and writing directly against a real host path.
That is the defining idea of bind mounts.

codeBlock.code: docker run -v /host/path:/container/path my-image

sections.title: Why Bind Mounts Matter
paragraphs: Bind mounts are especially useful when you want a container to work with files you care about on your machine.
Typical reasons include:
The key advantage is immediacy. Change the file on the host and the container sees it right away.

sections.title: -v /host/path:/container/path Syntax
paragraphs: The short syntax uses -v.
Inside the container, /app now points to the files from /Users/alex/project on the host.
This is different from named volume syntax:
That difference is subtle but critical. If the left side looks like a filesystem path, it is a bind mount. If it is just a name, it is usually a named volume.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it \
  -v /Users/alex/project:/app \
  node:20 bash

sections.title: --mount type=bind Syntax
paragraphs: The longer form is often easier to understand.
This has the same effect, but the fields are explicit:
Many teams prefer --mount in documentation and scripts because it reduces ambiguity.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it \
  --mount type=bind,source=/Users/alex/project,target=/app \
  node:20 bash

sections.title: Read-Only Bind Mounts with :ro
paragraphs: Sometimes the container should be able to read host files but not modify them. Bind mounts support this with the read-only flag.
Read-only mounts are useful for:
If a container only needs to consume a file, :ro is a very good habit.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  -v /Users/alex/config/app.conf:/etc/app/app.conf:ro \
  my-app

sections.title: Live Code Reloading: The Classic Development Pattern
paragraphs: One of the most common bind mount patterns is mounting your source code into a container that runs a development server.
Now your editor changes files on the host, and the container sees them immediately. If your framework supports hot reload or watch mode, the app reloads without rebuilding the image each time.
This is one of the biggest productivity advantages of bind mounts.
You could build a new image after each source edit, but that is slow and wasteful during development. Bind mounts create a fast feedback loop:
For frontend apps, API services, and local experiments, this workflow is extremely common.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it --rm \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  -v /Users/alex/myapp:/app \
  -w /app \
  node:20 \
  sh -c "npm install && npm run dev"

sections.title: Common Development Example
paragraphs: Here is a more complete example using a Python app:
The project directory on the host is mounted into /app. You can change app.py, templates, or configuration files locally while the container uses them.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it --rm \
  -p 8000:8000 \
  -v /Users/alex/python-api:/app \
  -w /app \
  python:3.12 \
  sh -c "pip install -r requirements.txt && python app.py"

sections.title: Security Considerations
paragraphs: Bind mounts are powerful because they expose real host files. That is also why they need caution.
If a bind mount is writable, the container can change, overwrite, or delete files on the host path.
That means a buggy script, a compromised process, or an accidental command inside the container can affect your local machine or server files directly.
Mount only what the container needs.
Less safe when unnecessary:
The broader the mount, the greater the risk.
If the container only needs to read a config file or certificate, use :ro.
Bind mounts are not inherently wrong in production, but they require stronger discipline because they depend on specific host paths and expose those paths directly to containers.

codeBlock.code: -v /Users/alex/myapp/src:/app/src

sections.title: Bind Mounts vs Named Volumes
paragraphs: These two storage patterns overlap in some use cases, but they are not interchangeable.
Use bind mounts when the host path itself matters.
Use named volumes when the data matters but the exact host path should be abstracted away.

sections.title: Common Use Case: Development Environments
paragraphs: Bind mounts are the default choice for local development because they keep your IDE, Git workflow, and container runtime connected to the same project directory.
Your code lives on the host, but the runtime tools live in the container. That is often the best of both worlds.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it --rm \
  -v /Users/alex/webapp:/usr/src/app \
  -w /usr/src/app \
  -p 5173:5173 \
  node:20 \
  sh -c "npm install && npm run dev -- --host"

sections.title: Common Use Case: Configuration Injection
paragraphs: Sometimes you want a containerized service to use a config file managed outside the image.
This lets you manage the config on the host and refresh the container without rebuilding a custom image.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  -v /Users/alex/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro \
  -p 8080:80 \
  nginx

sections.title: Common Use Case: Log Collection
paragraphs: Applications can write logs into a host directory for inspection or external collection.
Now tools on the host can process the logs directly.
This is useful, but be mindful of permissions and storage growth.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -d \
  -v /Users/alex/app-logs:/var/log/myapp \
  my-app

sections.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
paragraphs: Bind mounts revolve around paths, so path handling matters.
Absolute paths are the clearest and safest form:
There is no ambiguity about what is being mounted.

Relative paths may work depending on the shell and Docker tooling you use, especially in Compose or with commands executed from a known project directory. But they can also cause confusion because the meaning depends on the current working directory.
A common shell pattern is:
This expands to the current directory as an absolute host path.
Many bind mount bugs are not Docker bugs at all. They are path mistakes:
When in doubt, use an explicit absolute path.

codeBlock.code: docker run -v /Users/alex/project:/app my-image

sections.title: What Happens to Existing Container Files?
paragraphs: If the image already contains files at the container target path, a bind mount hides them while the mount is active.
For example, if the image has /app populated during build but you run:
the container sees the host folder contents instead of the original image files at /app.
This behavior surprises many beginners.
It is not merging. It is replacing what the container sees at that mount point.

codeBlock.code: docker run -v /Users/alex/empty-folder:/app my-image

sections.title: Permissions and Ownership
paragraphs: Permissions can become tricky with bind mounts because the files belong to the host filesystem, not to Docker. If the host user, host group, or container process user do not align, you may see read or write errors.
Common symptoms include:
The exact fix depends on your OS, Docker setup, and container user model, but the root cause is usually that bind mounts expose real host ownership rules.

sections.title: Practical Examples
paragraphs: In each example, the host path is intentionally part of the workflow.

codeBlock.code:
docker run -it --rm \
  -v /Users/alex/react-app:/app \
  -w /app \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  node:20 \
  sh -c "npm install && npm start"

sections.title: Best Practices
paragraphs: A smaller mount reduces risk and makes intent clearer.
If writes are not needed, prevent them.
They reduce ambiguity and surprises.
For durable application state, named volumes are often safer and cleaner.
Plan container paths accordingly.

sections.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: Mistaking a host path for a named volume or vice versa The syntax is similar, but the meaning is very different.
Mounting too much of the host This increases risk and makes containers less isolated.
Forgetting :ro for sensitive files Config and certificate mounts are often better as read-only.
Expecting bind mounts to be portable across machines The exact host path may not exist on another machine.
Overwriting expected image content with an empty host directory A bind mount hides the image files at the target path.

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: Bind mounts are one of the most useful Docker tools for real development work. They connect your host and your container directly, which makes local coding, live reloading, config injection, and host file access easy. That same power means you should use them deliberately: mount only what you need, prefer read-only when possible, and reach for named volumes instead when the real goal is persistent application data rather than host integration.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Docker bind mount?

A direct mapping of a host directory or file into a container, written as -v /host/path:/container/path. Unlike a named volume, you control exactly where the data lives and can edit it with normal host tools. The container sees changes on the host immediately and vice versa, which is what makes bind mounts the standard choice for local development with live reload.
When should I use a bind mount instead of a named volume?

Bind mounts for development, where editing source on the host and seeing it inside the container immediately is the whole point, and for mounting host configuration or certificates into a container. Named volumes for persistent application data such as database files, because Docker manages location and permissions, they are portable between hosts, and they perform far better on macOS and Windows. A rough rule: bind mounts for things you edit, named volumes for things the application writes.
Why are bind mounts so slow on macOS and Windows?

Because Linux containers do not run natively there. They run inside a Linux VM that Docker Desktop manages, and every file access crosses the boundary between the host filesystem and that VM. For a large project with many small files, such as node_modules, the overhead is substantial. Mitigations include mounting only the source directory rather than the whole project, using a named volume for dependency directories, and enabling VirtioFS in Docker Desktop settings.
Why are files created in a bind mount owned by root?

Because the container process runs as root by default, and a bind mount preserves real ownership on the host rather than remapping it. Files the container creates therefore appear as root-owned on your machine. Fix it by running the container as your own user, docker run --user $(id -u):$(id -g), or by setting a matching USER in the Dockerfile. This is a Linux-specific problem; Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows handles the mapping for you.
Can I make a bind mount read-only?

Yes, by appending :ro, -v /host/config:/etc/app:ro. The container can read the files but cannot modify them, which is the right setting for mounted configuration, certificates and any host path the application has no business writing to. It is a cheap safeguard, particularly when mounting something sensitive, and it prevents a compromised container from tampering with host files it can see.
Is it safe to bind-mount the Docker socket?

Rarely. Mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives the container full control of the Docker daemon, which on most setups is equivalent to root on the host. It can start a privileged container mounting the host filesystem. It is a common pattern for CI runners and monitoring agents, and it should be treated as granting host-level trust. Where possible use a socket proxy that restricts which API calls are permitted, rather than exposing the socket directly.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
paragraphs: Manage Docker volumes with docker volume ls, inspect, rm and prune. Learn how to back up a volume, restore it from a tar archive and migrate data between hosts.

Creating a volume is only the start. Real Docker work quickly becomes operational: you need to list volumes, inspect where data lives, remove abandoned storage, estimate disk usage, and sometimes back up or restore data before a migration. That is what volume management is about.
This lesson focuses on the Docker volume commands you use day to day. If named volumes give you persistence, volume management gives you control.

sections.title: Listing Volumes with docker volume ls
paragraphs: The first command to know is:
This lists all volumes Docker knows about on the current host.
You use docker volume ls to:
In busy development machines, the list often grows faster than expected.
Docker also supports filter flags with docker volume ls.
That helps narrow the list to volumes matching a condition, such as unused volumes.
Filters are useful when cleaning up large systems because they reduce the chance of deleting something important by mistake.

codeBlock.code: docker volume ls

sections.title: Inspecting Volumes with docker volume inspect
paragraphs: To see details about a specific volume:
The output is JSON and includes fields like:
Name tells you which volume you are looking at.
Driver tells you how Docker manages it. For most local systems, this is local.
Mountpoint shows where the actual data is stored on the Docker host.
Scope is usually local, meaning the volume belongs to the current Docker host.
If you ever need to answer “Where is my data?” or “Which driver is this using?”, docker volume inspect is the right command.

codeBlock.code: docker volume inspect pgdata

sections.title: Removing Volumes with docker volume rm
paragraphs: To delete one or more specific volumes:
This permanently removes the volume and its contents.
Docker does not remove a volume that is still in use by a container.
You may see an error like:
That happens when a running or stopped container still references the volume.
Before removing a volume:
The refusal to delete in-use volumes is a useful safety barrier, not an annoyance.

codeBlock.code: docker volume rm pgdata

sections.title: Cleaning Up with docker volume prune
paragraphs: Over time, unused volumes accumulate. To remove all volumes that are not currently used by any container:
Docker will ask for confirmation. To skip the prompt:
docker volume prune removes unused volumes, not every volume on the system.
That sounds safe, but remember: unused does not mean unimportant. A volume can be detached from containers and still hold valuable data you plan to reuse later.
Treat docker volume prune as a cleanup tool, not as a casual command.

codeBlock.code: docker volume prune

sections.title: Backing Up a Volume
paragraphs: Volumes are persistent, but persistence is not backup. If the disk fails or a volume is deleted, the data is gone unless you have copied it elsewhere.
A classic Docker backup pattern uses a temporary container to read the volume and create an archive on the host.
After the command finishes, myvolume-backup.tar.gz exists in your current host directory.

Docker volumes are managed by Docker, so you do not always want to manipulate their host storage paths directly. Using a helper container lets Docker handle the mount while you copy the data in a portable way.

codeBlock.code: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/myvolume-backup.tar.gz -C /data .

First, make sure the target volume exists:
Then restore the archive into it:
Now a container that uses myvolume can read the restored data.

paragraphs: Docker volume usage contributes to host disk consumption, but it is not always obvious how much. A helpful overview command is:
This shows disk usage for Docker objects such as:
Example conceptual output:
If your machine suddenly runs low on disk space, volumes are often part of the story. This command helps you identify whether local volumes are a major storage consumer before you start cleaning up.

paragraphs: Here is a safe volume management flow for a development machine:

sections.title: Common Scenarios
paragraphs: Docker says the volume is in use.
Interpretation: at least one container still references it. Find the container, decide whether it should keep the data, then stop or remove the container if deletion is truly intended.
If local volumes are large, inspect your active and dangling volumes. Old database experiments and Compose projects are common causes.
Back up the volume first. Even if the upgrade is expected to be safe, a quick archive is good insurance.
Back up, transfer the archive, create a volume on the destination, and restore.

codeBlock.code: docker volume rm pgdata

sections.title: Best Practices
paragraphs: Names like postgres-prod-data are easier to manage than vague names like data1.
If the data matters, archive it first.
A few seconds of inspection can prevent serious data loss.
Pruning is helpful, but only after you understand what is unused.
Docker storage grows quietly. docker system df gives you a quick reality check.

sections.title: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: Confusing persistence with backup A volume surviving container deletion does not protect against host failure or accidental removal.
Running prune without review Unused data may still be valuable.
Deleting a volume just because the container is gone The whole point of a volume is to outlive the container.
Ignoring disk usage until the host is full Storage problems are easier to prevent than to clean up under pressure.
Not testing restore procedures A backup only proves its value when it can be restored successfully.

sections.title: Final Takeaway
paragraphs: Volume management is what turns Docker storage from a mystery into an operational skill. Learn to list volumes, inspect them, remove them carefully, prune only with intent, and back them up before risky changes. If you can manage Docker volumes confidently, you are much better prepared to run stateful containers in both development and production.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I list and inspect Docker volumes?

docker volume ls lists them, and docker volume inspect <name> shows the driver, mountpoint and any labels. To see what is actually inside one without a running container, mount it into a throwaway container: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data alpine ls -la /data. That trick works for any volume regardless of platform, which matters on macOS and Windows where the real path lives inside the Docker VM and is not browsable from the host.
Why does docker system prune not remove my volumes?

Because volumes are excluded by default, deliberately. They usually hold the data you least want to lose. docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache, but leaves volumes alone unless you add --volumes. Use docker volume prune to remove volumes no container references, and check docker volume ls first, since a volume that looks unused may simply belong to a container you stopped.
How do I find which container is using a volume?

docker ps -a --filter volume=<name> lists containers referencing it, including stopped ones. docker volume inspect does not show consumers, which is a common source of confusion. This matters before pruning, since a volume attached only to a stopped container still counts as in use and will not be removed, while one whose container was deleted becomes eligible immediately.
How do I move a Docker volume to another host?

Archive it through a temporary container and transfer the archive: docker run --rm -v myvolume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tar.gz -C /data ., then reverse the process on the destination after creating an empty volume there. There is no built-in volume migration command. For databases, use the engine's own dump and restore rather than a filesystem copy, which can capture an inconsistent state if the database is running.
How do I reclaim disk space used by Docker volumes?

Start with docker system df -v, which breaks down usage per volume and shows which are unused. Then docker volume prune removes those with no container attached. Be deliberate. Unlike image pruning, this deletes data permanently and there is no recovery. Anonymous volumes created implicitly by images with a VOLUME instruction are a common hidden consumer, since each docker run creates a fresh one that nothing subsequently references.
What are anonymous volumes and why do I have so many?

When an image declares VOLUME /data and you run it without mounting anything there, Docker creates an anonymous volume with a random hexadecimal name. Every docker run creates another, so repeatedly starting such an image, database images commonly do this, leaves a trail of orphaned volumes holding real data. Mount a named volume explicitly to avoid it, add --rm which removes anonymous volumes on exit, and run docker volume prune periodically to clear the ones already accumulated.
